title_en: OpenAI now lets you text your Dot agent
title_fa: OpenAI now lets you text your Dot agent
excerpt_en: The feature works with both iMessage and RCS messaging.
excerpt_fa: The feature works with both iMessage and RCS messaging.
content_en:
OpenAI now lets you text your Dot agent
The feature works with both iMessage and RCS messaging.
When OpenAI debuted its Dot agents late last month, it promised users would eventually be able to text them to give them instructions. Now, nearly a month later, the company has begun rolling out a preview among US Pro users that allows you to do just that. With the new feature, OpenAI says you can send your Dot texts, photos and even voice memos. It also gives your Dot another avenue to proactively contact you with updates about tasks you've assigned to it.
By popular request, you can now text your dot.
Give it a task to take off your plate or something to keep an eye on, using text, photos, or even voice notes. It will text you proactively with relevant updates.
Safe, secure texting via iMessage or RCS. You're the only one who... pic.twitter.com/iuNd3aTCYc
— ChatGPT (@ChatGPT) October 28, 2026
To set up your Dot for texting, open its profile in ChatGPT and select Texting. Over on your phone, ensure iMessage is enabled if you're on an iPhone, and RCS if your daily driver is an Android device. OpenAI says it partnered with Linq to provide messaging support, and did "extensive" penetration testing to ensure the feature is safe. "You're the only one who can text your dot, and your dot can only text you," the company adds on X. Any information your Dot writes to its memory is shared across ChatGPT and text, meaning context carries over between different conversations.
The personal agent space is suddenly very hot after Anthropic joined last week with Claude Duet. In my testing, OpenAI's Dots are comparatively more polished. The fact that you can now text them is something I'm sure some people will appreciate. Using Claude Duet currently requires joining a waitlist that's only open to people in the US. Anthropic has said it plans to offer the agent to subscribers of its $20 per month Pro plan, which is not something you can say of Dots. They're currently not available to Plus tier users.

title_en: Wiz’s CTO on PHP2Shell and the coming ‘vulnpocalypse’
title_fa: Wiz’s CTO on PHP2Shell and the coming ‘vulnpocalypse’
excerpt_en: The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities...
excerpt_fa: The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities...
content_en:
The PHP scare may have faded from your feed, but the cleanup is far from over. Last week, two critical bugs in the open source language behind roughly 70% of websites left organizations scrambling to fix their systems, with some taking sites offline until the vulnerabilities could be patched. According to researchers who found the bugs, this is only the beginning, as AI changes how quickly novel vulnerabilities can be uncovered and exploited.
On this episode of TechCrunch’sEquity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Tomer Schwartz, CTO of Exposure Management & AppSec at Google-owned Wiz, who was part of the scramble — alongside OpenAI, research group Calif, and the PHP team — to fix the bugs. On the show, Schwartz and Bellan get into what the race looked like from the inside, how early-stage startups can build with security in mind, and why patching by hand won’t scale.
Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify, and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

title_en: Engadget is hiring writers!
title_fa: Engadget is hiring writers!
excerpt_en: We're looking for freelance journalists who know their way around a tech blog.
excerpt_fa: We're looking for freelance journalists who know their way around a tech blog.
content_en:
Engadget is hiring writers!
We're looking for freelance journalists who know their way around a tech blog.
Engadget has been covering the tech world for over 20 years, but there are only so many stories we can write in a given week. As such, we're hoping to add some contributing writers to our team.
We're searching for writers who know their way around the tech space and can turn around fast, clean copy. You don't need to know every facet of every topic we cover, but if you don't have a broad familiarity with the consumer tech space, this probably isn't the role for you. More than anything, we're looking for writers with the ability to distill complex subjects into stories that anyone can understand. While this shouldn't be your first writing gig, these are entry-level roles, and we value deep knowledge and enthusiasm for tech higher than a professional degree or decades of experience.
Engadget has a strict no-AI policy. Writers need to have a mastery of the English language, which includes the ability to write accurate, engaging and informative stories without the assistance of AI.
Provided you're not a robot, you'll be working with some of the most knowledgeable and experienced folks in tech journalism. Our news and features desks provide a steady stream of daily assignments, so there will always be fresh articles ready for you to tackle each day. Once you're up and running with a few articles under your belt, you'll be free to pitch and develop your own ideas, too.
Engadget is an entirely remote workplace. Our team is spread across four continents and can accommodate writers in any timezone. We offer either flat hourly or per-word rates, with the exact figures varying on experience. Any time you spend with Engadget, including training or trials, will be paid.
We pride ourselves on providing a friendly, collaborative and respectful working environment, with regular hours, regular assignments and regular pay. Many of our writers have been with us for years-– several of them over a decade — so we must be doing something right.
If the chance to have your work seen by the millions of readers who come to Engadget every month sounds like a dream, you can apply for a role here.

title_en: Sony's new see-through DualSense controllers let you game like its 1999
title_fa: Sony's new see-through DualSense controllers let you game like its 1999
excerpt_en: The company is also releasing matching PS5 console covers.
excerpt_fa: The company is also releasing matching PS5 console covers.
content_en:
Sony's new see-through DualSense controllers let you game like its 1999
The company is also releasing matching PS5 console covers.
Sony just announced some nifty-looking transparent DualSense PS5 controllers, recalling the glory days of the late 1990s and early 2000s when many tech gadgets boasted see-through designs. The Prism Collection will be available in three colorways, including orange, green and gray.
The company promises that each controller features a high-gloss clear finish that extends across the back, allowing users a peek into the tech that powers the DualSense. A company representative said that Sony "wanted to bring back the iconic see-through trend of the late '90s in a fresh, modern way that complements the PS5's industrial design."
The controllers are joined by console plate covers, which are available in the same three colorways. These go over the console, so they won't offer a glimpse into the internal workings of a PS5. Still, they match the controllers, which is fun.
Everything will be available to preorder directly from PlayStation beginning on November 10, with shipments going out in February. The DualSense controllers cost $85 and the console covers cost $75.
Sony first began dabbling in translucent controllers during the PS1 era. Since then, every PlayStation generation has gotten see-through gamepads at one point or another. Now it's the PS5's turn.

Sony first began dabbling in translucent controllers during the PS1 era. Since then, every PlayStation generation has gotten see-through gamepads at one point or another. Now it's the PS5's turn.

title_en: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro feels both familiar and radically improved
title_fa: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro feels both familiar and radically improved
excerpt_en: It's thinner, lighter and has a better screen - but it's still a MacBook Pro.
excerpt_fa: It's thinner, lighter and has a better screen - but it's still a MacBook Pro.
content_en:
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro feels both familiar and radically improved
It's thinner, lighter and has a better screen — but it's still a MacBook Pro.
As expected, Apple announced its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen at its "Pro and Tell" event today in Los Angeles. I've gotten a chance to quickly check it out the "MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display" and — it feels like a MacBook Pro. Apple didn't reinvent the wheel with this redesign, even though there are a ton of significant changes. The company kept the standard 14- and 16-inch screens, though the display has obviously been massively improved.
Despite the reduction in weight (the 14-inch is three pounds, while the 16-inch is four), Apple kept the same set of ports on these new models, and the keyboard and trackpad appear to be the same reliable and comfortable options that have been on the MacBook Pro since its big 2021 redesign. It's funny how shaving half a pound makes a huge difference, but it absolutely does in this case.
This isn't the first time that Apple has dramatically reduced the weight of the MacBook Pro — the infamous 2016 Touch Bar models were also about the same weight. But they also ran Intel chips and had notorious difficulty staying cool and performant under heavy work loads. I have to wager that won't be the case here, but it's definitely something we'll want to look out for when we do more in-depth testing.
The screen is a star
In 2024, Apple released the iPad Pro with its "tandem OLED" screen, one that I called the nicest display I had ever seen on an Apple device. Well, that title now goes to the MacBook Pro. The OLED technology makes for the blackest blacks, and the set of demo photographs and videos loaded on the laptop really show it off.
Using touch on the MacBook Pro works just as you'd expect. You can swipe through images, use two fingers for multi-touch gestures like panning and zooming, draw in apps like Pixelmator or adjust editing sliders in Photos. The UI has not significantly changed — you'd never know at first glance that this MacBook Pro was designed for touch. UI elements like the "stop light" buttons in the top left for window management expand slightly when you touch them, but there's otherwise no major concessions to this being an OS that supports touch.
The touch performance is pretty good, though I did feel like there were occasional stutters while switching between Spaces or full-screen apps. But I'm also chalking that up to the fact that I'm not at all familiar just yet with swiping and tapping in macOS just yet. The good news is that if you're familiar with gestures on your trackpad, like using a three-finger swipe to move between full-screen apps, those gestures work here as well. You can also "flick" apps to different sides of the screen to set up how your windows are laid out, something that you can already do on the iPad.
Ultimately, this is one of those expected product glow-ups where almost everything significant has changed, but it still feels perfectly familiar. That's a good thing: the 2016 major MacBook Pro revamp was one of the darkest moments for the Mac, as the company threw out too much of what worked while adding things of questionable value.
That's not the case here. The new MacBook Pro still has a great keyboard and trackpad, it still has powerful chips and plenty of ports. But the size and weight reduction is significant and the new display is extremely impressive (even if you don't use the touchscreen). Of course, this will cost you; Apple's highest-tech has never been cheap, and it's even worse than usual thanks to the ongoing storage and RAM crisis. But the $400 premium for these new laptops over the non-OLED verions at least feels justified.
Oh — and the glowing logo on the lid is just as cool now as it was 30-something years ago. I'm glad it's back.

title_en: Here's how the touchscreen on the MacBook Pro with PROLED display works
title_fa: Here's how the touchscreen on the MacBook Pro with PROLED display works
excerpt_en: The touch sensor isn't a separate layer of the screen.
excerpt_fa: The touch sensor isn't a separate layer of the screen.
content_en:
Here's how the touchscreen on the MacBook Pro with PROLED display works
The touch sensor isn't a separate layer of the screen.
A new touchscreen Mac requires new software, and with the announcement of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, Apple detailed just how you'll use your fingers to navigate macOS. The new laptop has an integrated touch sensor built directly into the display. Apple claims this reduces latency, making it "feel like you're touching the content itself." It's worth noting most modern OLED displays with touchscreens handle touch input this way.
As you would expect, you can slide your finger across the screen to scroll through content, and pinch with two fingers to zoom in on photos, documents and web pages. Additionally, it's possible to draw directly on the screen with a finger, allowing you to doodle and annotate notes. Apple suggests professionals will find the touchscreen useful for interacting with 3D objects and getting a feel for how their iOS apps will work, while for everyday users will appreciate it in apps like Pages and Keynote.
Borrowing a page from the iPad, you can use your finger to hide the dock. Likewise when you use touch to interact with menus, there's more spacing between items to make it easier to select a specific one. None of the above is groundbreaking, but it never hurts to have multiple ways to interact with a device.
The new MacBook Pro sees Apple finally embracing an idea it has spent nearly two decades calling misguided. Steve Jobs famously hated even the thought of adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, going so far as to say using one would be "ergonomically terrible." His successor, former CEO Tim Cook, joked creating a laptop with tablet-like features would be akin to making a fridge with a built-in toaster. Now it will be a question of whether people will want to spend at least $2,899 for the privilege of owning a touchscreen Mac before Apple trickles the feature down to its more affordable computers.

title_en: Apple launches its new touchscreen MacBook Pro
title_fa: Apple launches its new touchscreen MacBook Pro
excerpt_en: Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899.
excerpt_fa: Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899.
content_en:
After years of resisting, Apple today launched a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starting at $2,899. The release comes nearly 10 years after the company first tried integrating touchscreens on its laptops, with its Touch Bar on a MacBook Pro, which it later went on to remove.
The new MacBook Pro more fully embraces the touchscreen, offering a new PROLED XDR Display in both 14-inch and 16-inch screen sizes. The device is powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options to choose from, along with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 16TB of storage. The display has 2,000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
To make the new MacBook easy to use, Apple designed a hinge that stabilizes the screen when users touch it. This also helps to stabilize the camera when you are on a video call and trying to access content on the display.
In addition, the screen will include a Dynamic Island-style cutout instead of the notch that’s present on most of the current MacBooks. Plus, the new MacBook features a six-speaker array with a new woofer design for better sound.
The 14-inch Pro weighs 3.0 pounds (1.38 kg), and the 16-inch Pro weighs 4.0 pounds (1.82 kg) — lighter than its non-touch predecessors.
Both feature three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe, and a headphone jack. Users can hook up three external displays on the M5 Pro variant and up to four displays on the M5 Max variant.
The Touchscreen MacBook Pro 14-inch starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch version starts at $3,399.
Consumers can place a preorder for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro from October 30, and the device will be available starting November 6.
The new Touchscreen MacBook marks two marquee product launches for new CEO John Ternus, who also introduced the company’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, in September. Various Apple executives, including Steve Jobs and Tim Cook, have scoffed at the idea of a touchscreen Mac in the past. Jobs famously called the idea “ergonomically terrible” at one point. However, rumors of the company working on such a variant started circulating nearly three years before today’s introduction.
The launch follows yesterday’s unveiling of a new standard MacBook Pro with the M6 chip in 14-inch size starting from $1,999.

title_en: Apple's redesigned MacBook Pro has an OLED touchscreen, weighs just three pounds
title_fa: Apple's redesigned MacBook Pro has an OLED touchscreen, weighs just three pounds
excerpt_en: It could use a more distinctive name, though.
excerpt_fa: It could use a more distinctive name, though.
content_en:
Apple's redesigned MacBook Pro has an OLED touchscreen, weighs just three pounds
It starts at $2,899, and it could really use a more distinctive name.
What's better than a MacBook Pro? A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen. Apple finally announced its long-rumored redesign today, and for the most part, it seems like the company went out of its way to create its most premium laptop yet.
The new MacBook Pro has a refined design that's noticeably thinner than the existing models, has slimmer bezels and the aforementioned touchscreen. But, similar to the recent RTX Spark Windows laptops, you'll need deep pockets if you want one: The 14-inch model starts at $2,899, making it the highest launch price we've ever seen for a MacBook Pro. The 16-inch model is even wilder, starting at $3,399.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, as it's officially called, is powered by either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, just like the non-touch models. And as a nice throwback to older Apple laptops, its rear Apple logo also lights up. As part of the new design, the OLED MacBook Pro features a Dynamic Island around its webcam, and Apple claims the 14-inch model weighs just three pounds. That's a noticeable difference from the current MacBook Pro, which clocks in at 3.4 pounds. The 16-inch model weighs four pounds, whereas the non-touch 16-inch MacBook Pro weighs between 4.7 and 4.8 pounds.
The ProLED XDR screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, according to Apple, and it features an "industry-leading" 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. I can only imagine the eye-searing possibilities with this screen. It also features a 120Hz refresh rate, just like existing MacBook Pros. Thanks to the slimmer bezels, Apple was also able to squeeze in larger 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens.
Beyond the new specs, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR doesn't look much different from Apple's current lineup. And thankfully, you've still got a useful array of ports: three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C connections, MagSafe, HDMI, headphone jack and an SDXC card slot.
So what's the point of a touchscreen MacBook Pro? It makes the simple act of casually scrolling through articles and content easier, as we've seen on touchscreen-equipped Windows PC over the last 15 years. But in the demo video above, we can also see people swiping on media and manipulating 3D objects. It also looks like you can interact with iOS apps just as they would with a phone, which would be particularly useful to developers. Apple says its own apps are optimized for the new MacBook Pro's touchscreen, and you'll be able to touch any app because macOS recognizes touch interactions as clicks. Third-party creator apps like Notion, Canva, Powerpoint and Blender will also work with the touchscreen natively.
There's no doubt Apple is late here, but there was also a certain wisdom in completely separating its touchscreen platforms (iOS, iPadOS and watchOS) from macOS, a platform that was designed entirely around traditional computer inputs. With Windows 8, Microsoft rushed to enable PC touchscreens as a way to compete with the potential rise of iPads. Apple didn't have the same pressure — especially since its glass touchpads offer an incredibly smooth scrolling experience on Macs.
MacBook Pros were always expensive, especially after Apple's recent hikes, but the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR pushes cost to a new extreme. A fully-decked out 16-inch model with an M5 Max chip, 128GB of RAM and 16TB of RAM costs an eye-watering $14,549. It's clearly not meant for a regular consumer. But given the rise in demand for powerful local AI hardware, I wouldn't be surprised if there's a robust market for an over-equipped MacBook Pro OLED.

title_en: Fake PS5 emulators on GitHub are spreading password-stealing malware
title_fa: Fake PS5 emulators on GitHub are spreading password-stealing malware
excerpt_en: This is according to the threat research arm of NordVPN.
excerpt_fa: This is according to the threat research arm of NordVPN.
content_en:
Fake PS5 emulators on GitHub are spreading password-stealing malware
This is according to the threat research arm of NordVPN.
Fake PS5 emulators infected with malware have been floating around GitHub, according to an investigation by NordVPN. The company's Threat Intelligence research team found that the malware is disguised as legitimate emulation software and works to steal passwords and other personal data.
The listing pages mimic existing emulation software, which is likely to trick people into thinking they're downloading the real thing. As of this writing, malicious GitHub repositories have been disguised as the popular Kyttyps5 and AnyPS5 emulators.
"Emulation fans are a perfect target. They are used to downloading experimental software from GitHub and running unsigned files, so nothing about this feels suspicious," says company CTO Marijus Briedis. "But this is not an emulator. It steals your data, hides from your antivirus and erases its own tracks before you notice anything is wrong."
Here's how it works. Once downloaded, the malware adds exclusion rules to Microsoft Defender, so it'll never be scanned by antivirus software. Next, it deploys an executable file NordVPN believes is an infostealer that scoops up passwords and anything else it can get its hands on. Finally, the software runs a cleanup script that deletes its own files. The PC's owner would never know it was there and what it did. Scary stuff.
The best way to avoid the issue is to double and triple check that the GitHub link you're downloading from is affiliated with the project team behind the emulator. Be wary of lookalikes with recent creation dates and a small number of reviews. Also, do not disable antivirus software throughout the download and installation process.
Sony announced earlier this year that it would no longer be officially porting its first party games to PC. This could account for the recent popularity of emulators like Kyttyps5.

title_en: Xreal Aura is a new wired headset powered by Android XR
title_fa: Xreal Aura is a new wired headset powered by Android XR
excerpt_en: Xreal Aura will start at $1,279 and will have multiple XR specific apps at launch.
excerpt_fa: Xreal Aura will start at $1,279 and will have multiple XR specific apps at launch.
content_en:
At the Android Dev Summit on Wednesday, Google’s smart glasses partner Xreal launched its new Xreal Aura wired smart glasses, powered by the Android XR and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite platforms. The companies had teased the glasses earlier in the year at Google’s I/O developer conference.
As Meta expands its push into smart glasses, competitors like Apple and Google are keen to release their own devices. Much like it did with Android smartphones, Google is relying on an assortment of partners, including Samsung and Xreal, to bring devices powered by its Android XR platform to consumers.
The new Xreal Aura smart glasses are tethered to a smartphone-like device for processing power, rather than handling all the computing themselves. The glasses then display the content in the wearer’s field of view.
The device’s design, meanwhile, is closer to Meta’s smart glasses than Apple’s Vision Pro, which is a larger headset.
Xreal Aura uses Sony’s Micro-OLED display with 1200p resolution at 120 Hz and a 95-degree field of view — screen specs that put the glasses above the Ray-Ban Meta Display on paper. However, Xreal’s smart glasses are heavier at 95 grams compared to Meta’s 69 grams, and you have to carry the puck.
At launch, the Aura supports many popular Google Play apps and games along with specific XR experiences, including the NBA App for Android XR; Nevatars; Fallout: Factions; Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars; the NASCAR XR App; and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s “The Nutcracker.”
Users can opt to plug a computer or handheld gaming console directly into the Xreal Aura via USB-C to make it an augmented display. The device can also allow for various entertainment and productivity use cases by spinning up a multimonitor setup or a big virtual screen.
For audio, the Xreal Aura uses Bose’s tech to power its sound while watching videos or listening to music.
Given that the new smart glasses are powered by Android XR, Gemini is available to users as a Q&A assistant and can help them understand on-screen context.
The Xreal Aura is available to order starting today in the United States, Canada, Japan, and
South Korea. The 12GB + 256GB version costs $1,279 with a limited launch price of $1,099 through December, and the 16GB + 512GB version is priced at $1,499 with a launch price of $1,299 through December. The company said it will start shipping by mid-November.
In May, Xreal CEO Chi Xu told TechCrunch that building a smart glass business is hard and everyone is losing money. He also said that the Aura glasses will have a wide range of use cases, and the industry has reached an inflection point of having the right hardware, software, and design smart glasses to reach scale.
“You need all the key pieces ready — you need the hardware ready, the operating system needs to be ready, and then you need a great user interface,” Xu said at that time.

Xreal Aura uses Sony’s Micro-OLED display with 1200p resolution at 120 Hz and a 95-degree field of view — screen specs that put the glasses above the Ray-Ban Meta Display on paper. However, Xreal’s smart glasses are heavier at 95 grams compared to Meta’s 69 grams, and you have to carry the puck.
At launch, the Aura supports many popular Google Play apps and games along with specific XR experiences, including the NBA App for Android XR; Nevatars; Fallout: Factions; Project Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars; the NASCAR XR App; and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s “The Nutcracker.”
Users can opt to plug a computer or handheld gaming console directly into the Xreal Aura via USB-C to make it an augmented display. The device can also allow for various entertainment and productivity use cases by spinning up a multimonitor setup or a big virtual screen.
For audio, the Xreal Aura uses Bose’s tech to power its sound while watching videos or listening to music.
Given that the new smart glasses are powered by Android XR, Gemini is available to users as a Q&A assistant and can help them understand on-screen context.
The Xreal Aura is available to order starting today in the United States, Canada, Japan, and
South Korea. The 12GB + 256GB version costs $1,279 with a limited launch price of $1,099 through December, and the 16GB + 512GB version is priced at $1,499 with a launch price of $1,299 through December. The company said it will start shipping by mid-November.
In May, Xreal CEO Chi Xu told TechCrunch that building a smart glass business is hard and everyone is losing money. He also said that the Aura glasses will have a wide range of use cases, and the industry has reached an inflection point of having the right hardware, software, and design smart glasses to reach scale.
“You need all the key pieces ready — you need the hardware ready, the operating system needs to be ready, and then you need a great user interface,” Xu said at that time.

title_en: As AI agents reshape the web, Google opens Gemini and Search to more apps
title_fa: As AI agents reshape the web, Google opens Gemini and Search to more apps
excerpt_en: A new developer platform will let businesses bring their services to Google's AI experiences, potentially changing how consumers discover and use apps.
excerpt_fa: A new developer platform will let businesses bring their services to Google's AI experiences, potentially changing how consumers discover and use apps.
content_en:
Google is making it easier for businesses to connect their apps to its AI experiences across Search and Gemini with the debut of its Connected Apps Platform.
Introduced in Gemini and Google Search earlier this year, connected apps let users securely link and interact with popular third-party services, then use them to take specific actions. For instance, you could connect to Canva to design a flyer, or to YouTube Music to build a playlist.
We’ve seen varying takes on the idea by other consumer-facing AI services like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse. The premise is that such integrations could ultimately shift consumer behavior away from launching and using individual apps to instead using their favorite services through their preferred AI provider.
However, to successfully capture and retain consumers’ attention, there have to actually be a wide range of connected apps to explore.
Google’s idea is to open its doors to any business or developer that wants to reach users through Search or Gemini by allowing them to submit their own connected apps and monitor their performance.
The platform preview is currently available in beta to developers in the U.S., and will allow developers to build and submit apps that can be used across Google’s products.
To get started, developers would integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app, Google explains.
Essentially, this process lets devs connect their app to Google’s services so it can be used with the search giant’s AI features. Developers can also choose whether they want their app to be available via Search, the Gemini app, or both.
After the app is live, developers can track traffic, latency, and error rates, and maintain control over their brand identity, such as their verified logos and authenticated accounts.
Similar to how SEO allowed companies and websites to show search engine rankings, this could well be one of the initial steps for businesses that want their services to be more visible to users on the agentic web.
Google already has over 50 Connected Apps available in Gemini, including from partners like Adobe, Experian, Localiza, Peloton, and others, in addition to its own expansive set of services, from Workplace and Photos to YouTube Music and Google Home.
These apps will now come to Google Search over the next few weeks. Search today has fewer integrations, featuring apps like Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football, and others.
Google said meditation app Calm is another new partner on this effort, and that its app will soon launch on both Gemini and Search.
The new Connected Apps platform is in public preview for U.S. developers who sign up for the waitlist. Google did not share when it would become more broadly available.

title_en: Chrome’s AI-powered Autofill can now dig through your Gmail to fill out forms
title_fa: Chrome’s AI-powered Autofill can now dig through your Gmail to fill out forms
excerpt_en: The autofill update lets Chrome pull flight confirmations, tracking info, order details, and other information from your inbox, with your permission.
excerpt_fa: The autofill update lets Chrome pull flight confirmations, tracking info, order details, and other information from your inbox, with your permission.
content_en:
Google’s Chrome browser is getting an update that will improve its autofill capabilities using AI. On Wednesday, the company said that Chrome will get an advanced version of autofill that will help users fill out online forms with suggestions pulled from their Gmail.
That means Chrome could suggest things you might need to know, like a flight confirmation number, membership ID, tracking information, order number, address, phone number, or credit card number by referencing your email.
The update is an expansion of Google’s Personal Intelligence, which already allows users to connect their Google Apps to its AI assistant, Gemini, to retrieve certain details and then use them to answer complex questions.
Though seemingly minor, the update could make Chrome easier to use, which could give users another reason to continue to use Google’s browser and stay in its AI ecosystem. It’s reminiscent of one of Apple’s most appreciated features: the ability to automatically detect verification codes sent via text and display them above the keyboard, allowing users to enter them with a single tap.
As with other Personalized Intelligence features, users can decide whether or not to enable enhanced autofill from their Chrome settings. Sensitive data is encrypted, Google notes.
The feature is rolling out to U.S. users on the desktop, and in the iOS and Android apps for Gemini in Chrome.

title_en: The Xreal Aura smartglasses are now on sale for a discounted launch price
title_fa: The Xreal Aura smartglasses are now on sale for a discounted launch price
excerpt_en: The new wearable is the first of its kind to run on the Android XR platform.
excerpt_fa: The new wearable is the first of its kind to run on the Android XR platform.
content_en:
The Xreal Aura smartglasses are now on sale for a discounted launch price
The new wearable is the first of its kind to run on the Android XR platform.
The Android XR-powered Xreal Aura smartglasses are now available to buy, and if you order a pair before the end of the year you can get them for a discounted price.
Xreal first unveiled the Aura earlier this year at Google I/O. They're the first wired glasses to utilize the Google and Samsung co-developed XR (extended reality) OS, and run Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.
Key to the Aura's appeal is their lightweight build. They weigh in at under 95g and look like a slightly chunkier version of a regular pair of glasses. The tradeoff is that they have to be tethered to a separate puck for battery and compute purposes. The external device also features a built-in trackpad and fingerprint sensor.
Xreal is pitching the Aura as a true do-it-all spatial computing wearable for work, entertainment, gaming and general AI-assisted tasks. Gemini is built into the OS, and you'll have access to 150 dedicated XR experiences out of the box, as well as all your standard day-to-day Google Play apps.
Among the made-for-XR games are the puzzler Cubism and a virtual version of the Fallout tabletop game Fallout: Factions. GameSir has worked with Xreal on a gamepad designed specifically for the Aura, which is equipped with a dedicated Gemini key that allows Google's chatbot to be immediately summoned mid-game. The company has also announced a wireless portable keyboard, and you can plug in your laptop or PC gaming handheld via USB-C. External devices appear in your spatial workspace alongside the built-in apps.
The Aura smartglasses have a 70-degree field-of-view, Micro-OLED displays and a resolution of 1200p at 120Hz. Bose handled tuning on the built-in open-ear speakers.
You can pick up the 12GB + 256GB model for $1,099 through December. It usually costs $1,279. The ordinarily $1,499 16GB + 512GB variant costs $1,299 for the remainder of 2026. Shipping is expected to begin in the middle of November.

title_en: New York governor signs AI chatbot child safety law
title_fa: New York governor signs AI chatbot child safety law
excerpt_en: A separate law aims to shore up security on connected baby monitors.
excerpt_fa: A separate law aims to shore up security on connected baby monitors.
content_en:
New York governor signs AI chatbot child safety law
A separate law aims to shore up security on connected baby monitors.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a law that aims to protect children from AI chatbot harms. The legislation requires AI companies to verify users' ages. They'll need to offer users at least one verification method that doesn't entirely rely on government ID. Companies will have to delete this "age information" after use.
If a user is under 18 or a company has yet to confirm the person is an adult, their chatbot will need to abide by certain restrictions. For instance, it cannot pretend "to be a real person, to be alive or to have human emotions." According to a press release, the legislation also bans chatbots from:
-
Claiming a personal, romantic, professional or authority-figure relationship with a child
-
Unprompted emotional questions, and using a child's private health or personal information from earlier conversations
-
Promoting or helping with suicide, self harm, eating disorders or drug and alcohol use
-
Encouraging kids to keep secrets, isolate themselves or avoid asking parents, trusted adults or professionals for help
-
Any sexually explicit content or child sexual abuse material
There will be a website through which the public can file complaints to New York's attorney general. Companies that break the law may be on the hook for civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, as well as damages, restitution and other forms of relief. They may also have to delete any data they collect unlawfully along with models trained on that information. The law will take effect in six months.
"Under this new law sponsored by Senator Gonzalez and Assemblymember Bores, no longer will minors have access to chatbots that pretend to be their friends and boyfriends and girlfriends," Hochul said at a press conference. "No longer will chatbots be allowed to keep sensitive information about a minor's emotional and physical health. No longer will chatbots discourage kids from seeking help from licensed professionals. And I'm not sure why we have to pass a law against something so obvious, but no longer will minors have access to chatbots that may in any way encourage thoughts of suicide. Now, this law builds on our groundbreaking Safe for Kids Act that sent a message loud and clear to technology companies: We will not allow you to monetize our children's mental health."
"New York just made history by signing into law the strongest kids' AI safety bill in the country," Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of Common Sense Media, said in a statement. "AI companies offer chatbots with features that are dangerous, and even deadly, for kids and teens. That is not innovation; it is reckless endangerment of our children. Now, those harmful features will be outlawed in New York."
Steyer added that the legislation is a template for the rest of the US. Earlier this month, eight states filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI, accusing the company of endangering children.
In September, New York City banned public schools from letting children from 2-K to eighth grade access generative AI tools in class. There are some exceptions, including for those who require assistive technology. During the one-year ban, the city will carry out studies into the impact of the tech on children.
Hochul also signed legislation that will require baby monitors with an internet connection that are sold in the state to prevent unauthorized users from seeing or hearing any activity that the devices capture. These baby monitors will also need to have warning labels that remind users why it's important to use security features and highlight the risks of unsecured connections. The law takes effect in 90 days.

title_en: Reddit is the latest platform to embrace the ‘For You’ feed
title_fa: Reddit is the latest platform to embrace the ‘For You’ feed
excerpt_en: The For You feed combines posts from communities users have joined with recommendations tailored to their interests.
excerpt_fa: The For You feed combines posts from communities users have joined with recommendations tailored to their interests.
content_en:
Reddit is the latest social platform to adopt the “For You” feed popularized by TikTok. The company announced on Wednesday that users will now see two options when opening the platform: “For You” and “Following.”
The “For You” feed combines posts from communities users have joined with recommendations tailored to their interests. Reddit says the feature will help users discover relevant communities and conversations they might not have otherwise come across. The “Following” feed only displays posts from communities they have joined.
The company says the change is designed to foster connection, participation, and belonging.
Reddit is likely hoping that the redesigned feed experience will nudge users to engage with content beyond the communities they already follow. It also brings Reddit more in line with the recommendation-driven experience that’s become standard across social media, where algorithms play a significant role in shaping what users see.
With the launch, Reddit joins a number of popular platforms that have adopted “For You”-style feeds, including Instagram, X, Threads, and Facebook.
Of course, not everyone will welcome the change, as some users may prefer the more focused feed experience of only seeing posts from communities they’ve joined, rather than having recommended content mixed into their home feed. Some users who encountered the new feed during its initial testing phase have already expressed their frustration with the change.
Reddit says users can switch between feeds and return to the one they last viewed the next time they open the platform.
It’s worth noting that although Reddit has long recommended posts from outside users’ subscribed communities, the new layout gives those recommendations their own feed on the homepage.
“This new feed experience is a first step in helping drive discovery that leads to something novel and relevant – an idea, a connection, a unique perspective, or even a new interest,” the company wrote in a blog post. “A more human internet is not just something you sit back and watch, it is something you find value in and want to participate in.”
The new feed experience is rolling out globally over the next few weeks, the company says.

title_en: Reddit is adding a 'for you' feed for recommendations
title_fa: Reddit is adding a 'for you' feed for recommendations
excerpt_en: The app will have a "following" tab to surface content from subreddits you've joined.
excerpt_fa: The app will have a "following" tab to surface content from subreddits you've joined.
content_en:
Reddit is adding a 'for you' feed for recommendations
The app will have a "following" tab to surface content from subreddits you've joined.
Reddit is changing up its main feed as it looks to emphasize more recommended content. The platform is splitting its feed into "for you," which will surface algorithmic recommendations, and "following" which shows posts from subreddits you've joined.
The change makes Reddit's central feed more like other mainstream social platforms. Up until now, the company has had one main feed that mixes in recommended posts alongside updates from subreddits you've joined. The new "for you" section will be more focused on allowing users to "discover relevant communities and conversations you might not otherwise come across," the company said in an update. With the change, Reddit will initially open to the new "for you" feed, but it will default to whichever feed you were last using the next time you launch the app.
The company is likely hoping the move will boost users' engagement with the platform. CEO Steve Huffman has said he wants to make it easier for casual users to come back to the service and that Reddit should find more ways to surface relevant posts, even if they are older. The company is also experimenting with video and audio versions of popular posts, some of which are from threads that are several years old.
So far, the company hasn't put those posts into a full-screen scrollable TikTok-like feed. But in its blog post announcing the change, Reddit said that it would "continue experimenting with ways people can more intentionally explore Reddit," including "new ways to navigate" the app. The company also said it's working on ways for users to offer feedback on recommended content to make it easier to fine tune its suggestions.

title_en: AI execs may be too out of touch to build for the general public
title_fa: AI execs may be too out of touch to build for the general public
excerpt_en: Tech leaders are flaunting how out of touch they are when they brag about using AI to connect with their families.
excerpt_fa: Tech leaders are flaunting how out of touch they are when they brag about using AI to connect with their families.
content_en:
Former Yahoo CEO and early Google engineer Marissa Mayer is catching a lot of flak for how she uses AI. In an interview about her new app Dazzle, an AI assistant that learns from your camera roll, Mayer poses what she believes is an impressive flex for the product: It helped her come up with three bullet points about her 10-year-old daughter for a birthday presentation at school, describing her as “empathetic, creative, and an animal lover.”
It’s a vague description, like a generic horoscope — it could probably describe a lot of 10-year-olds.
Some onlookers, like progressive activist Leah Greenberg, marveled that “the fact that Marissa Mayer would voluntarily disclose this to a reporter is a pretty good demonstration of how deeply the culture of Silicon Valley has diverged from the rest of humanity.”
Perhaps Mayer drew so much backlash because we have repeatedly observed sheltered billionaires suggest that we outsource child-rearing — one of life’s greatest tests of patience, humility, and kindness — to a computer that is incapable of understanding human emotion.
We’ve been primed for this frustration. Last year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Bored Ape owner and late night host Jimmy Fallon on national television, “I cannot imagine … figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT.” The public didn’t love that comment, either, but Altman wasn’t fazed by the negative feedback. A few months ago, he said on X that a “cool use case” of ChatGPT Work would be creating a podcast that talks about your kids’ upcoming birthdays or soccer games and “explain[s] your kids’ interests.” (He was brutally ratioed with comments like, “What if you just talked to your children?”)
After publication, Mayer defended herself in a long X post. She claims she was not relying on Dazzle to explain her child to her, but rather, she was testing what her prototype could do — it resurfaced photos of “forgotten kindergarten projects,” like a “snake devenomer” or “sandcat playground,” illustrating her daughter’s creativity and care for animals.
Fair enough. But Mayer remarks in the same interview that people could also use her AI to outsource the mental load of “figuring out the theme for your child’s birthday party.” She says she’s used her app to plan a playdate for her daughter, book family activities on vacation, and decide what to be for Halloween. She even proposes that her AI assistant could coordinate plans with her husband’s AI assistant. When the reporter asks her if it’s depressing to imagine this “frictionless future … planned by AI,” Mayer replies, “I haven’t really thought that through.”
These leaders seem to write off the naysayers as part of a small, angry fringe group. Yet a Pew Research Center study reports that 50% of U.S. adults think that AI will reduce people’s ability to form meaningful relationships. Only 5% of respondents said AI would make it easier to build these connections.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, however, joins his Silicon Valley kin in envisioning a world where our social needs are met via AI.

title_en: Trump DOE loans $5B to nuclear plants that will power data centers
title_fa: Trump DOE loans $5B to nuclear plants that will power data centers
excerpt_en: Constellation Energy will get $5 billion in government loans to modernize nuclear reactors. Most of the new capacity is already committed to Google, Amazon, and Meta.
excerpt_fa: Constellation Energy will get $5 billion in government loans to modernize nuclear reactors. Most of the new capacity is already committed to Google, Amazon, and Meta.
content_en:
The Trump administration is giving Constellation Energy $5 billion in loans to expand nuclear generating capacity at eight power plants by 1.1 gigawatts.
Most or all of the additional power from seven of those facilities has already been bought by Google, Meta, or Amazon.
Constellation said it plans to use the financing to “uprate” 11 existing reactors, an industry term for expanding capacity at a reactor, often by using more highly enriched uranium and by upgrading equipment to handle the increased power levels.
The energy company said it had already committed to spending more than $7 billion to add 1,080 megawatts of nuclear capacity to deliver power to Google, Amazon, and Meta. The loan commitment, which has yet to be finalized, “could lower financing costs” for the projects, Constellation said in a press release.
The eight power plants include six in Illinois (Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, La Salle, and Quad Cities), one in Maryland (Calvert Cliffs), and one in Pennsylvania (Limerick).
Google is already the confirmed buyer of additional power from the Pennsylvania plant and four Illinois power plants, while Amazon is buying electricity from the Maryland plant and Meta is effectively buying the entire Clinton power plant in Illinois.
On Tuesday, the Department of Energy touted the loan as supporting “affordable, reliable power to American homes and businesses,” though there is no evidence that the new nuclear capacity will lower prices for residential ratepayers. Constellation’s announcement does not say whether the projects will maintain or lower electricity rates, and the company would not confirm the government’s claim to TechCrunch.
Hyperscalers, including Google, Amazon, and Meta, have been scouring the grid for additional capacity to support their AI data centers. Tech companies are paying handsomely for energy, committing tens of billions of dollars over the coming years. Given that power has become a competitive advantage, that estimate is probably on the low end.
By lowering the cost of capital for the upgrades, the Department of Energy’s loans could boost Constellation’s bottom line, that of the hyperscalers — or both.

title_en: South Korea’s financial industry hit by fresh wave of cyberattacks
title_fa: South Korea’s financial industry hit by fresh wave of cyberattacks
excerpt_en: South Korea’s financial institutions have been hit by another wave of cyberattacks, highlighting the growing risk of AI-driven hacking in Asia.
excerpt_fa: South Korea’s financial institutions have been hit by another wave of cyberattacks, highlighting the growing risk of AI-driven hacking in Asia.
content_en:
South Korea’s financial institutions have been hit by another wave of cyberattacks, highlighting the growing risk of AI-driven hacking in Asia. The latest incidents affect brokerages Daishin Securities and Mirae Asset Global Investments, as well as the crypto exchange Bithumb.
The incident comes roughly a month after a series of cyberattacks targeting South Korean financial institutions, raising concerns about vulnerabilities beyond just the country’s banking systems. Security researchers linked the September wave of attacks on South Korea to a suspected China-based hacker who relied on an AI penetration testing tool called Artex, though officials are still investigating the root cause of the latest breaches.
According to local news, Daishin reported a cyberattack that exposed the personal information of 38,490 customers, including names, email addresses, and mobile phone numbers. The company has notified affected customers, is cooperating with authorities in the investigation, and will compensate for any losses as required by law.
Meanwhile, Mirae and Bithumb reported separate cybersecurity incidents on Wednesday, per local media, though neither has confirmed that customer data was taken.
South Korea’s financial regulator has called for stronger cybersecurity measures following a string of attacks on financial firms and government agencies, per officials in Seoul on Wednesday. The country also plans to conduct security checks on dozens of IT systems in the private sector.
Yesterday, Japan reported a cybersecurity incident involving GMO Internet, following a series of attacks on its financial institutions. The wave of cyberattacks across Asia underscore growing cybersecurity challenges in the region, often as a result of years of weak cybersecurity; though, investigators have not established a connection between the incidents.
South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC), Daishin Securities, Bithumb, and Mirae Asset Global Investments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

title_en: Audio Technica just released its first set of wireless StreamSet headphones
title_fa: Audio Technica just released its first set of wireless StreamSet headphones
excerpt_en: This expands the lineup beyond XLR and USB-connected models.
excerpt_fa: This expands the lineup beyond XLR and USB-connected models.
content_en:
Audio Technica just released its first set of wireless StreamSet headphones
This expands the lineup beyond XLR and USB-connected models.
Audio Technica just released a wireless model in its popular StreamSet category of headphones. The new ATH-M50xSTS-WL is the very first wireless version in the lineup.
These cans don't connect via Bluetooth, as StreamSet headphones are primarily intended for content creators, streamers and gamers, all of which require ultra-low latency. They connect via 2.4GHz, so there's a USB transceiver that hooks up to PCs and gaming consoles like the PS5 and Switch 2. The battery lasts for around 24 hours and is charged via USB. The headphones can still work while being charged, via a wired connection.
Otherwise, these are extremely similar to the original wired ATH-M50xSTS headphones. They feature microphones based on the company's 20 Series and audio drivers pulled from the ATH-M50x professional monitor headphones.
The headset includes adaptive noise cancellation with two selectable levels. The company says an algorithm "continuously monitors audio input to prioritize the user's voice over ambient sounds," which includes stuff like PC fans and air conditioners.
There's a cardioid condenser microphone on a flexible boom arm that instantly mutes audio when flipped up. It uses the same 45mm audio drivers found in the ATH-M50x studio monitor headphones. I've used that particular and iconic model and can attest they do indeed sound great.
They ship with two types of interchangeable earpads. There's a pair for better sound quality, which is great for listening to music, and another designed with breathable mesh for long streaming and gaming sessions. The ATH-M50xSTS-WL headphones are available right now and cost $299.

title_en: Voice AI in vogue: Nvidia releases new open transcription model
title_fa: Voice AI in vogue: Nvidia releases new open transcription model
excerpt_en: Nvidia just released a free speech-to-text model that can transcribe up to 40 languages, but it only works on recordings, not live audio, so it’s a big step for meeting and medical transcription tools while still leaving real-time use to rivals like ElevenLabs.
excerpt_fa: Nvidia just released a free speech-to-text model that can transcribe up to 40 languages, but it only works on recordings, not live audio, so it’s a big step for meeting and medical transcription tools while still leaving real-time use to rivals like ElevenLabs.
content_en:
Nvidia on Wednesday released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, a free, open-weight model that transcribes audio in up to 40 languages. It also released version 2 of Granary, its open source speech dataset.
Nvidia boasts that Nemotron 3.5 can translate 31 languages to and from English, handle recordings up to an hour long, and tell up to eight speakers apart. It claims to beat rivals on benchmarks, including Hugging Face’s Open ASR Leaderboard.
These tools target developers building apps for business meetings and medical transcription, two of AI’s most established footholds in the workplace. Nvidia says developers can use the model, the updated Granary dataset, and tools like its NeMo Speech model to customize apps to recognize an industry’s jargon in each language. One drawback: Transcribe works with recorded audio, not livestreams.
Still, the company promises Transcribe, at 30 billion parameters, can run on a single chip, from the Jetson AGX Thor robotics controller and DGX Spark chip powering new laptops, to Blackwell datacenter chips. It joins Nvidia’s open-weight voice models, including the super small yet powerful Parakeet (1.1 billion parameters).
Nvidia’s latest voice entry comes during a busy period of AI voice releases: Mistral shipped Voxtral 3 earlier this month; ElevenLabs launched Realtime for instant speech in voice agents; and Salesforce released Launa-Omni, its voice model.

title_en: Amazon debuts the Alexa Photo Frame and Echo Time smart clock, plus other upgraded devices
title_fa: Amazon debuts the Alexa Photo Frame and Echo Time smart clock, plus other upgraded devices
excerpt_en: Amazon's other new devices include an upgraded Echo Dot, an Echo Studio with visual intelligence features, and the Echo Show 16.
excerpt_fa: Amazon's other new devices include an upgraded Echo Dot, an Echo Studio with visual intelligence features, and the Echo Show 16.
content_en:
Amazon unveiled five new Alexa devices today, including two new kinds of hardware: the Alexa Photo Frame, a smart picture frame, and the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock.
The Alexa Photo Frame is Amazon’s foray into the world of digital photo displays, a product category that has transcended from a clunky, last-minute holiday gift to a sleek, attractive way to look through your camera roll.
Aura is responsible for much of the growth in this category, so it’s no coincidence that the Alexa Photo Frame has a similar aesthetic feel: The screen is much easier on the eyes than the old, bright photo frames from years past. The device is said to be specifically calibrated for sharing photos, featuring a semi-matte, anti-glare display that makes it look more like a Samsung Frame TV than a laptop screen.
Also like Aura, the Photo Frame’s 10-inch screen looks like a matte photograph, helping it blend in with other artwork on your wall.
Amazon’s new device, though, adds the value of integration with users’ existing Amazon accounts. Prime members get unlimited storage on Amazon Photos, and Alexa+ is supposed to intelligently choose how and when to display photos.
“It knows to choose photos where you’re smiling and the lighting is right, and it matches the season you’re in, so you see last year’s family Halloween costumes in October instead of the middle of spring. It also knows what to skip, like screenshots and receipts,” Amazon said in a press release. You can also add voice notes to photos, and images sync automatically as you take them.
The Alexa Photo Frame is on sale now, and starts at $199.99 in Black, and $229 in Birch or Walnut wood.
Meanwhile, the Echo Time clock seems to be a response to the growing sentiment that people don’t want to rely on their phones for alarms, setting morning reminders, or checking the weather.
“Millions of customers start and end their days with Alexa — checking the weather and turning on the lights from bed in the morning or winding down with white noise at night,” Amazon wrote. “But the bedroom asks for something different from a device than the kitchen or living room does — so we designed an Echo specifically for it.”
Amazon says that the Echo Time, which costs $199.99, or $209.99 for a Kids version, has opt-in sleep sensing tools. You can choose to set a smart alarm feature that wakes you up within a 10 to 60 minute window of your alarm time, and can wake you when it detects you’re in a lighter phase of sleep, so that it’s less jarring to begin your day.
Like the popular Hatch alarm clocks, the clock can also mimic sunrise features to ease you awake.
Amazon also showed off updates to its existing lines of devices. We now get the Echo Show 16, a new Echo Dot, and Echo Studio with Home Camera.
The biggest upgrade to the Echo Dot is that it now includes a built-in smart home hub, which also includes an eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 1,000 square feet of coverage, helping it connect to lights, locks, and thermostats around your home. The new Echo Dot is also powered by Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon chip, which is said to make it better at on-device processing to speed up conversations with its AI, Alexa+.
Amazon says its most advanced speaker, however, is the Echo Studio with Home Camera. This speaker doubles as a camera so you can check on your home while you’re out, and also has visual intelligence features.
“Alexa can also see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help you in real time,” Amazon explained. “Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.”
The Echo Dot is available at $99.99, and the Echo Studio with Home Camera costs $249.99.
Finally, Amazon unveiled the new Echo Show 16, which includes a 16-inch display. Amazon says the device has a 10% larger viewing area than its predecessor, but with a 40% smaller frame. It has Fire TV built in, plus Smart Home tools like Family Organizer. It can also function like a digital photo frame.
The Echo Show 16 is available for preorder for $499.99.

title_en: TikTok expands into restaurant guides with ‘Must Eat’ feature
title_fa: TikTok expands into restaurant guides with ‘Must Eat’ feature
excerpt_en: The move puts TikTok in more direct competition with platforms like Yelp and Google.
excerpt_fa: The move puts TikTok in more direct competition with platforms like Yelp and Google.
content_en:
TikTok has long been a go-to place for discovering new spots, with viral videos helping local restaurants attract new customers. Now, TikTok is making it easier for users to find their next favorite restaurant with a new feature called “Must Eat.”
Introduced Wednesday, the community-driven guide highlights restaurants getting attention on the platform, bringing food recommendations from across the U.S. into one place.
The move puts TikTok in more direct competition with platforms like Yelp and Google Maps. But instead of relying mainly on search results, maps, and traditional reviews, TikTok is building on what it already does well: connecting people with restaurants through recommendations shared by other users.
“Must Eat” uses more than 40 million posts and comments to pull restaurant recommendations and curated lists together in one place. Users can browse restaurants by city and filter results by cuisine, price, rating, and location, making it easier to compare options before heading out.
The recommendations are split into two categories: “Everyday Eats,” featuring casual favorites and neighborhood go-tos, and “Elevated Dining,” highlighting restaurants for celebrations, special occasions, or a night out.
Additionally, select restaurants can be booked directly through TikTok via OpenTable.
The feature is launching first in New York City, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. Users can find it through the search bar, the Local feed, restaurant pages, and location links attached to videos featuring participating restaurants.

title_en: FCC clears Amazon Leo to acquire mobile-satellite operator Globalstar
title_fa: FCC clears Amazon Leo to acquire mobile-satellite operator Globalstar
excerpt_en: Amazon Leo's $11.5 billion acquisition of mobile-satellite operator Globalstar has been approved by the FCC.
excerpt_fa: Amazon Leo's $11.5 billion acquisition of mobile-satellite operator Globalstar has been approved by the FCC.
content_en:
FCC clears Amazon Leo to acquire mobile-satellite operator Globalstar
The deal is designed to allow Leo to to deliver direct-to-device service.
Amazon Leo's $11.5 billion acquisition of mobile-satellite operator Globalstar has been approved by the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the regulator announced. The deal is designed to expand Leo's space-based footprint and allow direct-to-device service for its growing satellite network, Amazon previously said.
"The companies' complementary assets promise to enhance Amazon Leo's entry into the direct-to-device segment and create a stronger satellite operator capable of offering fixed and mobile services to residential, business, and government customers," the FCC wrote in a press release that echoed Amazon's own talking points. The regulator said that the deal is likely to benefit the public by enhancing data coverage in underserved areas.

title_fa: Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition 2026 review: Nice, but doesn't justify the price
excerpt_en: $320 is a lot to pay for a well-balanced device in an aluminum case with pogo pins.
excerpt_fa: $320 is a lot to pay for a well-balanced device in an aluminum case with pogo pins.
content_en:
Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition 2026 review: Nice, but doesn't justify the price
$320 is a lot to pay for a well-balanced device in an aluminum case with pogo pins.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
I'll be honest. I don't have much to say about the new Kindle Colorsoft. It doesn't feel like that long ago that Amazon introduced its first-ever color ereader, but that was in October 2024. At the time, the product was novel for the company, as it presented a technical challenge. How was Amazon going to offer a paper–like color reading experience while preserving the quality of a black-and-white ereader? The company used nitride LEDs and custom algorithms to finetune how lights were beamed through individual pixels to maintain contrast levels, and also made sure that pages turned faster than previous devices. The original Colorsoft only came in one color, which felt like a staid container for its relatively vibrant contents.
Cut to October 2026 and Amazon has a new Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition for the world. It's a bit thinner than before, with edge-to-edge color and a new color option: Fig. With this variant, the Colorsoft's front bezels also match the rest of the case, so you won't see unsightly white or black bars like on previous models. This Kindle Colorsoft generation starts at $290, but if you pay $30 more, you can get the Signature Edition, which is what I'm reviewing here.
What's new (or not so new) in the Kindle Colorsoft 2026?
Everything else about the Kindle Colorsoft is basically the same as its predecessor. You're still getting a screen with 300 pixels per inch (ppi) for black-and-white reading, or 150 ppi for color. Nothing has changed about the color representation here – you still get the "vibrant" mode in addition to the standard rendering to get a bit more saturation out of your pages.
I'm not a huge graphic novel reader, and most of the pops of color in my Kindle Colorsoft experience are in the book covers in my Library or when I highlight particular sentences or passages. They were pleasant little touches, but for me, the novelty of paperlike color E Ink displays has largely worn off. If I'm not reading something where the colors are actually integral to the storytelling, I don't need an ereader to deliver a broad spectrum of shades.
All that is to say – the reading experience on the Kindle Colorsoft this year is largely the same as last year, minus the early troubles our reviewer (and some other people online) encountered with yellow bands on their devices. Since Amazon resolved to fix the issue, it should not impact current and new Colorsoft models, and I did not notice this during my testing. I didn't experience any obvious issues when reading on the Colorsoft either.
Pricing is a bit confusing to compare, so bear with me. At launch in 2024, Amazon only made a "Signature Edition" of the Colorsoft available, and it started at $280. This year, the Colorsoft starts at $290 for the base configuration with 16GB of RAM and goes up to $320. That additional spend will get you the Signature Edition's aluminum case, pogo pins on the back, twice the storage and the choice of black or maroon. So you can say the Colorsoft costs between $10 and $40 more than before, and for that money you're mostly getting a slightly more refined flush-front design and thinner chassis.
In real life, much as I appreciated the aesthetic tweak, it didn't have a huge impact on my reading experience. I never struggled to hold the previous Colorsoft (or many other recent Kindles) so the thinner body, while nice, wasn't a huge change. The new Fig finish was a nearly identical match for my Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro, though, so if you love matching your gadgets to each other, this might be worth considering.
More importantly, I liked the sturdiness and premium vibe of the aluminum housing. My Kindles live in my cluttered purses, and their ability to withstand scratches is crucial. In my two weeks with the new Kindle Colorsoft, I've thrown it in my backpack with no regard for its safety, and it's still managed to remain pristine. I did decide to put a case on it midway through my testing so as not to tempt the review Gods, though, to ensure I could get a good photo of it before my recklessness marred it forever.
Charging and battery life
I haven't had a chance to connect the Colorsoft to any new accessory that's compatible with its new pogo pins in the real world yet. But I can at least say that based on a short demo ahead of Amazon's launch, I enjoyed how easy it was to snap the Signature Edition Colorsoft onto a magnetic case and use page turning buttons on a cover that connected via the pogo pins. I'll need more time to judge the responsiveness, consistency and ease of use, but for now, color me intrigued. I do wish Amazon hadn't removed the ability to wirelessly charge the Colorsoft. It's so handy to just drop the tablet onto a charging stand, and those who have already bought those accessories might be miffed at the omission.
That said, I never worried about charging the Kindle Colorsoft, because like most other Kindles, its battery lasts forever. I mean quite genuinely, because every time I pick up one of the many abandoned Kindles lying around in my house, they always still have juice left. I was slightly concerned when, after a day or two of focused reading, the Colorsoft's battery dipped by 10 percent to 90 percent. But then I remembered I had the same experience with the larger, more energy intensive Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. And that thing remains alive on my couch without me even thinking about plugging it in.
I won't say that I've had enough time to properly evaluate the Kindle Colorsoft's battery performance, but suffice it to say that nothing in my two weeks with it has been a real cause for concern so far.
The competition
Like I said, I don't read a lot of stuff that's better in color. But I can tell you that the Kindle Colorsoft is not your only option out there...

title_en: Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026) review: Updated in all the right places
title_fa: Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026) review: Updated in all the right places
excerpt_en: Amazon's updates to the Paperwhite Signature Edition make it feel even more premium, but the regular version remains a great choice for less money.
excerpt_fa: Amazon's updates to the Paperwhite Signature Edition make it feel even more premium, but the regular version remains a great choice for less money.
content_en:
Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026) review: Updated in all the right places
Are you willing to pay $50 more for the upgrades?
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
There's no denying the chokehold Amazon has on the ereader industry. Its library is massive and its entire lineup of Kindles are consistently reliable devices that meet readers with varying budgets and needs. As part of the company's 2026 lineup, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition ($250) sits squarely in the middle in terms of both capabilities and price. Amazon saw fit to refine an already compelling mix of design and performance, with key changes to how you use this Paperwhite as well. But as we noted with the 2024 Signature Edition, the best premium ereader may not offer any exclusive features that you can't live without.
Design changes
Amazon didn't try to reinvent the wheel with its updates to the more premium Paperwhite. There's now an aluminum back, but overall, it's still an IPX8 waterproof design with a high-contrast, 300 dpi display (more on the screen changes later) and 32GB of storage. The company did color match the front bezels on the Seaglass Green version so it matches the back panel. This is certainly a welcome change as it definitely looks better than previous models that had colorful cases but with gray fronts. The 2026 model is also one millimeter thinner than its predecessor — a variation you're unlikely to notice, but one Amazon will gladly tout.
Amazon also moved the power button to the top right edge, a location that will be more familiar for anyone who uses a smartphone. I honestly prefer it there, because even though I've been using a regular Kindle Paperwhite since 2024, I never got used to the power button on the bottom edge. Now, the USB-C port is the only component that still resides there.
Perhaps the biggest change on the 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition is the introduction of pogo pins on the back cover. Amazon ditched the 2024 model's standard wireless charging (via Qi-compatible and Amazon accessories) in favor of this arrangement. The four pins accommodate new accessories, most notably the Page Turn Cover ($80) with physical page-turn buttons, and there's also a $60 charging stand with an unknown shipping date. I should note that both of these accessories also work with the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, which has the requisite pogo pins onboard as well.
Reading experience
In my opinion, the Paperwhite line offers the best reading experience on a Kindle. I don't need a color screen, but I do prefer the adjustable warm light and larger display over the standard Kindle. Of course, the IPX8 waterproofing is also nice to have, as I like to take the Paperwhite to the beach, and you can certainly feel safe using it during a bath or at the pool.
To further enhance the overall experience, Amazon employs an oxide-thin film transistor backplane and offers a contrast ratio that it says is its highest yet. The company promises deeper blacks and crisper text on the 2026 Signature Edition compared to the previous version, although my eyes are unable to discern the difference in either of those. I couldn't distinguish between the sharpness on my 2024 Paperwhite and this new Signature model either, but I could tell them apart by the slightly warmer overall glow of the latest release, even when the Warmth slider on both Paperwhites was set to 0. Still, the Paperwhite display continues to offer the best ereader performance among the company's lineup for my money.
The auto-adjusting front light feature returns, using an ambient sensor to increase the brightness in daylight or dim it at night without you having to do so yourself. Of course, you can disable this feature and swipe the slider as you see fit. There's also a new double tap gesture that allows you to turn pages by double tapping on the left and right sides. Two taps on the right edge to go to the next page, or two taps on the left to go back. I didn't use this very much, probably because I'm conditioned to just tap once on the sides of the display to turn pages (which still works here). I'll also mention there's an accelerometer in this 2026 version for automatic screen rotation, but I don't have much use for it, so I left rotation locked during the bulk of my testing.
One area I wasn't able to test in the two weeks I've been using the new Paperwhite Signature Edition is battery life. Amazon says you can expect up to 12 weeks of battery life on a charge, and with past Kindle devices, I've left them unused for months and come back to enough juice for multiple reading sessions. Simply put, Kindles last for what seems like forever, and that's not going to change here.
My 2024 Paperwhite has never been sluggish when it comes to downloading books or searching, but the 2026 Signature Edition seems to be slightly quicker with both of those tasks. They both wake up with equal quickness though, which is more important to me than how adept these devices are at navigating menus.
Kindle alternatives
If you don't like the Paperwhite, there's likely to be something else to suit your needs in Amazon's own lineup. Of course, the company's advantage over other ereaders is its massive library that's accessible right on its Kindle devices. There's also the Kindle Unlimited Kindle+ subscription that gives you access to millions of books, magazines and comics for $12 a month. That integration and convenience gives Amazon a leg up on its competition.
If you prefer a non-Amazon ereader, the most recent one we've tested is the Boox Go 6 (Gen II). The Android-based device gives you access to more reading apps than a Kindle would, plus there's a microSD card slot and stylus support. This model has shorter battery life than some ereaders and there's no water resistance, so there are some trade-offs. I'll also note that we named the Kobo Clara Colour the best overall ereader in our buyer's guide. You do have to contend with a limited...
