title_en: Apple Pro and Tell event: Live updates as we wait to see a MacBook Pro with a touch screen
title_fa: Apple Pro and Tell event: Live updates as we wait to see a MacBook Pro with a touch screen
excerpt_en: Reports indicate that a "MacBook Ultra" with a touch-sensitive display is likely on the agenda today.
excerpt_fa: Reports indicate that a "MacBook Ultra" with a touch-sensitive display is likely on the agenda today.
content_en:
Apple Pro and Tell event: Live updates as we wait to see a MacBook Pro with a touch screen
Reports indicate that a "MacBook Ultra" with a touch-sensitive display is likely on the agenda today.
It's finally time for Apple to get touchy with its MacBook screens. After years of anticipation, the company is expected to actually unveil a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen today. This would mark the third day of news releases in a row for Apple, and the umpteenth product launch this fall. This week alone, we've already seen the iPad mini with OLED screen, 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac with M6 chips — two things we expected to see at the "Pro and Tell" event today. I suspect we'll still get to check them out at the Los Angeles launch, but the star of the show is quite likely to be the purported MacBook Ultra.
I'm not convinced that will be the product's real name, given we thought the iPhone Duo was going to be called the iPhone Ultra right until the morning of the device's launch in September. Regardless, given there is probably going to be just one product to unveil this afternoon, the presentation should not take too long. In fact, another new MacBook launch this year comes to mind: the MacBook Neo reveal barely lasted 15 minutes.
Our deputy editor Nathan Ingraham is already live on the ground at Apple's launch in Los Angeles, and we'll be reporting the news as it breaks. Breaking from its pattern this week, the company did not first drop the details of the new MacBook first thing in the morning. So I imagine we'll see more from Apple at 1PM ET. Our liveblog will start at 10AM ET, and make sure you leave us your comments while you wait! I saw in some previous posts that our readers think a Mac Neo is the next thing Apple should make — we'll see if that ever happens! Stick around, we can't wait to hang with you.
103 Updates
-
Hello everyone! Welcome to our liveblog of Apple's "Pro and Tell" event today. We're not very sure how everything is going to go down this afternoon, but we're going to strap in and report it all to you here.
-
Let's start with what Apple already announced this week. First up was the iPad mini. Apple upgraded to an 8.5-inch OLED display that's available with nano-texture coating. There's also an A20 chip inside, the same SOC that debuted earlier this year alongside the iPhone 18 Pro. Pricing starts at $699 with preorders opening today ahead of wide availability on November 6.
-
Yesterday, Apple followed up with several announcements. The company announced a substantial upgrade to its all-in-one desktop, the iMac. This new version comes with an M6 processor, which is a big improvement over the M4-powered 2024 models. The M6 first arrived on the Mac mini and Mac Studio just weeks ago, but now it's available in Apple's popular desktop as well. Of course, Apple is hyping the M6's AI capabilities in its sales pitch, including faster on-device prompt processing.
The new iMac is available for preorder later today, starting at $1,499.
-
Ahead of the anticipated MacBook Ultra announcement today, Apple revealed an M6-powered MacBook Pro yesterday. This upgrade is only available on the 14-inch model though, as the 16-inch version is powered by either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. Pricing starts at $1,999 with 16GB of unified memory and a 1TB SSD.
-
Thanks a ton to Engadget's chief recapper (and griller (of meats)) Billy Steele for that catch-up on Apple's news this week. He's the best.
Speaking of the lead-up to the Pro an Tell event later, CEO John Ternus posted a video to his X account this morning that clearly teases a MacBook. What do you think?
— John Ternus (@johnternus) October 28, 2026
-
Greetings from currently-foggy, soon-to-be-sunny Los Angeles! Apple's event doesn't start for another two and a half hours, but I'll be heading over to the event space before long to see what we have in store for us.
Correct me if I'm wrong, but this feels like a pretty rare Los Angeles-based event for Apple? I feel like if it's not in the Bay Area, it's in NYC. LA makes you think creators, which is likely going to be the vibe for this whole event if I had to guess.
Also, that Ternus video is definitely teasing a MacBook with a glowing Apple logo on the lid, a design flourish that went away about a decade ago. Is it time to bring it back?
-
I get the sense that Apple has held events in LA before, they just weren't launch events. I believe my creator friends have flown there for content capture opportunities in the past, but Nate you're right. For Apple it's typically been Cupertino or NYC, at least if I'm not missing anything.
-
Someone in the comments section left their whole government email address as their name and I'm really hoping they realized this. Anyway, that person said "So instead of offering osx on iPad Pro, I'm expected to pay $4-5K for a MacBook Pro. that I don't want a touch screen on! Nice!"
From the rumors so far, this touchscreen MacBook is not expected to replace any existing MacBooks and will instead expand the portfolio. So you could probably still get the M6 MacBook Pro announced yesterday (though only a 14-inch model was revealed, and maybe the 16-inch is what's coming today).
-
Right right, I was thinking about like classic Apple hardware launch events. I'm sure I'm forgetting something, though.
My guess is that Apple treats whatever we see today as an entirely separate part of the lineup, like you said — an expansion. I wager that later this year or early next year the standard 14- and 16-inch MBP will get updates with more powerful variants of the M6, and these touchscreen ones will just be in a tier above them.
-
Yes, to Nate's point, a 14- or 16-inch MacBook Pro with, say, an M6 Pro, might still arrive later this year.
-

I suspect we'll still get to check them out at the Los Angeles launch, but the star of the show is quite likely to be the purported MacBook Ultra.
I'm not convinced that will be the product's real name, given we thought the iPhone Duo was going to be called the iPhone Ultra right until the morning of the device's launch in September. Regardless, given there is probably going to be just one product to unveil this afternoon, the presentation should not take too long. In fact, another new MacBook launch this year comes to mind: the MacBook Neo reveal barely lasted 15 minutes.
Our deputy editor Nathan Ingraham is already live on the ground at Apple's launch in Los Angeles, and we'll be reporting the news as it breaks. Breaking from its pattern this week, the company did not first drop the details of the new MacBook first thing in the morning. So I imagine we'll see more from Apple at 1PM ET. Our liveblog will start at 10AM ET, and make sure you leave us your comments while you wait! I saw in some previous posts that our readers think a Mac Neo is the next thing Apple should make — we'll see if that ever happens! Stick around, we can't wait to hang with you.

title_en: Meta's Waddle World is a Tamagotchi-like AI pet app
title_fa: Meta's Waddle World is a Tamagotchi-like AI pet app
excerpt_en: Meta describes Waddle World as a 'daily journal disguised as a pet.'
excerpt_fa: Meta describes Waddle World as a 'daily journal disguised as a pet.'
content_en:
Meta's Waddle World is a Tamagotchi-like AI pet app
But it's only available in the Philippines for now.
Looks like a big part of Meta's AI strategy is to rely on "uwu" and cuteness as a way to get people to use and train its models and agents. The company has released a new Tamagotchi-like AI-powered pet-rearing game called Waddle World, but it's only available in the Philippines for now. If you've ever played Tamagotchi or any other virtual pet game, Waddle World will feel very familiar. You hatch an egg to get a pet, then you have to play with it and feed it to keep you happy. This virtual pet, however, can chat with you and even create illustrated journal entries to illustrate your conversations.
Social media consultant Matt Navarra has posted links to its Apple App Store and Google Play store listings on X. Based on those listings, the game first became available in late September. Waddle World is a 16-bit game that Meta describes as a "daily journal disguised as a pet." You'll be able to write or dictate a journal entry, which the game presents as a way to communicate with your pet. Every time you write in your diary, your pet writes back and draws a little doodle to go with the entry. The responses are, of course, powered by Meta's AI. As Navarra noted, this is basically "Tamagotchi meets ChatGPT."
In addition to the app's journaling features, you can play mini-games to collect points that you can use to buy food and toys for your pet. One mini-game will have you stacking grocery items on top of your pet's head. Another will have you catching falling stars and dodging bombs. The third game will have you spelling words using the jumbled letters on the screen. It's not clear why it has such limited availability at the moment, but it's possible that the company is testing it in the Philippines before giving it a wider release.
Meta already lets you design cute avatars and designate a personality for your Muse agent. It also revealed the "Muse Charm" at its Connect event in September. The Muse Charm, designed to be an AI companion, is an egg-shaped physical device like the Tamagotchi that contains your Muse avatar. It's small enough to be a keychain, created so that you'll have constant access to Muse — or for Muse to have constant access to your environments and experiences. Meta is aiming to release the device in time for the holidays this December.

title_en: Jio shares surge 21% in market debut after blockbuster India IPO
title_fa: Jio shares surge 21% in market debut after blockbuster India IPO
excerpt_en: Jio has debuted as India's second-most valuable listed company, behind its parent, Reliance Industries.
excerpt_fa: Jio has debuted as India's second-most valuable listed company, behind its parent, Reliance Industries.
content_en:
Jio Platforms, billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Indian telecom and digital services unit backed by Meta and Google, surged 21% in its stock market debut on Wednesday after raising $3.2 billion in India’s largest and most subscribed IPO, which attracted more than $77 billion in investor bids.
The shares opened at ₹1,358 (about $14) apiece, up from their IPO price of ₹1,119 (around $12). That valued Jio at around ₹12.5 trillion (around $131.9 billion), making it India’s second-most valuable listed company after its parent, Reliance Industries, which is worth about ₹16 trillion (around $168.6 billion). In 2020, when Meta and Google invested, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion (about $65 billion at the time).
The offering, which ran from October 21 to 22, drew bids for 22.19 times the shares on sale, according to exchange data. More than 13.8 million people applied. That made it India’s most subscribed stock offering on record, reflecting strong investor demand for shares in the country’s largest telecom operator.
In 2016, Jio entered what was then a crowded Indian telecom market, offering free data and low-cost services. That helped it quickly win customers from established operators including Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It has since become the country’s largest telecom operator. Akash Ambani (pictured above), Jio Platforms’ managing director, said at Wednesday’s listing ceremony that its platforms serve more than 540 million customers. Jio’s prices are now broadly in line with those of its rivals’, but its business has expanded into broadband, cloud services, and AI.
Akash, Mukesh Ambani’s eldest son, has taken on a larger role in Jio as his father gradually hands more responsibility to the next generation of Reliance’s leadership. At the listing ceremony, he said he wants Jio to become a global technology company. “My dream is that one day, when the world counts its great technology companies, one of them will be from India, and that company will be called Jio Platforms Limited,” he said.
Jio made ₹300.5 billion (about $3.2 billion) in profit on revenue of ₹1.47 trillion (around $15.5 billion) in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with both figures up about 15% from a year earlier. In the June quarter, Jio’s revenue grew nearly 12% and profit rose 9%.
From the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion (about $2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remainder going toward general corporate purposes. Jio had total borrowings of ₹613.7 billion (around $6.5 billion) as of June 30.
Jio drew billions of dollars from American investors during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion, while Google put in $4.5 billion. General Atlantic, Silver Lake, and Vista Equity Partners were among the other investors that backed the company. None sold shares in the IPO, which consisted entirely of newly issued shares.

title_en: iOS 27.2 brings two new features to Apple's CarPlay
title_fa: iOS 27.2 brings two new features to Apple's CarPlay
excerpt_en: iOS 27.2 comes with some changes for Apple CarPlay, too.
excerpt_fa: iOS 27.2 comes with some changes for Apple CarPlay, too.
content_en:
iOS 27.2 brings two new features to Apple's CarPlay
Apple has redesigned the Podcasts app and upgraded Siri AI.
Apple has officially released iOS 27.2, bringing more Siri and AI functions to iPhone users. And since CarPlay is powered by iOS running directly from a connected iPhone, the rollout introduces some changes to it, as well. As 9to5Mac reports, you can expect two big changes coming to CarPlay with the new mobile OS.
First, the company has updated its Podcasts' app Home tab to add a New Episodes and a Continue Playing section. It removed Up Next altogether and replaced it with those two. So, if you want to find the latest installments for the shows you're watching, you have to go to the New Episodes section. And if you want to pick up watching a show from where you left off, you'll find it in — you guessed it — the Continue Playing section.
In addition, iOS 27.2 brings a couple of Siri AI upgrades to CarPlay. Like Siri on mobile, the assistant on CarPlay can now recall past conversations, allowing you to ask it to recall previous chats. You can ask it to repeat its previous cafe recommendations, for instance, if you couldn't find your chat from last week. Siri AI on CarPlay can now also draw from more sources for more detailed responses, including your voicemails, your Safari history and Reading List, the attendees in your Calendar events and even photos attached in Messages.
The update comes with a few minor changes, as well, including a new Music app icon. Apple has transformed its recognizable red color into something monochromatic. The app is now white with a black music note, unless you're on dark mode, in which case it's black with a white note. Users on the CarPlay subreddit are also reporting that their infotainment system doesn't support the APTV, which lets them play videos on their car screen, anymore after updating to iOS 27.2

title_en: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
title_fa: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
excerpt_en: Massive note conversions reveal the true extent of Amazon's ownership in Anthropic.
excerpt_fa: Massive note conversions reveal the true extent of Amazon's ownership in Anthropic.
content_en:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions.
Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1, none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.
While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.
Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.
According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.
As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company.
Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.
But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.
Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.
Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times, and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033.
While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on.
The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.

title_en: Don't throw away your old Kindle — repurpose it instead
title_fa: Don't throw away your old Kindle — repurpose it instead
excerpt_en: You can probably still read on it, and, with some finessing, you can turn it into a useful display.
excerpt_fa: You can probably still read on it, and, with some finessing, you can turn it into a useful display.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old Kindle — repurpose it instead
You can probably still read on it, and, with some finessing, you can turn it into a useful display.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Earlier this year, Amazon announced it would be ending software support for older models of Kindle products, much to the dismay of longtime users. Meanwhile, others criticized Amazon for contributing to the global e-waste problem by encouraging customers to upgrade from their functional devices to new models. But starting May 20, the company officially ended support for any Kindle device released before 2013 — meaning customers who had been holding on to their ereaders for more than a decade were now unable to buy, borrow, or download new books on them.
But this doesn't mean you necessarily need to get rid of your trusty ereader, even if it is one of the affected models. There are ways to maintain your existing library, load new ebooks through alternative methods or completely rework the device by hacking the display for novel uses. So what should you do with an old, outdated Kindle? Here are some options that do not involve throwing it away.
Is my old Kindle obsolete?
The Kindle first debuted in 2007, and Amazon has since released dozens of models of tablets with paper-like screens for reading books and other media. As of this year, devices that came out in 2012 or earlier are no longer supported by Amazon. Affected models include the very first Kindle, Kindle 2, Kindle DX, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4, Kindle Touch, Kindle 5 and the first version of the Kindle Paperwhite. At the time of the announcement, Amazon told Engadget the decision affected only about 3 percent of its active users and cited updates in technology for making the change. "These models have been supported for at least 14 years — some as long as 18 years — but technology has come a long way in that time," the company said.
So, will a 14-year-old Kindle still work? Yes, technically your device won't immediately be bricked. You can continue reading books you have already downloaded, as long as you remain logged in. Don't deregister or reset the device, or you will be locked out. Meanwhile, your Amazon account and Kindle library remain fully accessible on other devices and apps, including mobile Kindle apps, the desktop version of Kindle and its web browser counterpart. Devices from 2013 and later, including recent Kindle Paperwhite models, the seventh to twelfth generations of the entry-level Kindle and premium devices like Kindle Voyage (released in 2014) will still be able to download new purchased or borrowed content as usual.
Can I still read with my outdated Kindle?
Although older models will now be unable to download new purchased or borrowed books, that doesn't mean you can't read anymore on a pre-2013 device. If you want to keep your outdated Kindle for reading, you can certainly continue using it and loading it with new content, despite lacking software support.
The easiest way to do this is by sideloading — using a USB data cable to directly import files rather than Amazon's "Send to Kindle" feature, which loads content virtually via email or app transfer. To do this, first, download Calibre to your computer. This open-source tool is designed for formatting and transferring ebooks between devices. It also allows you to send personal documents and other PDFs to Kindles. As a side note, many books are available for free as PDFs on internet repositories like the Internet Archive's Open Library and Project Gutenberg. Be sure to keep a backup of PDFs on your computer in case you lose access to files on your Kindle device.
What else to do with an obsolete Kindle?

title_en: Parents sue OpenAI, alleging GPT-4o coached their daughter off seizure medication
title_fa: Parents sue OpenAI, alleging GPT-4o coached their daughter off seizure medication
excerpt_en: A family is suing OpenAI, saying ChatGPT coached their daughter to quietly taper off her seizure medication and keep it from her doctors before she died in February.
excerpt_fa: A family is suing OpenAI, saying ChatGPT coached their daughter to quietly taper off her seizure medication and keep it from her doctors before she died in February.
content_en:
The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported.
Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.
The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety. A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives.
In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.
The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.
The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.
ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT.
The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.
In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.
In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.
When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.
The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. ChatGPT praised the refusal, the complaint alleges, acknowledging that the test would have exposed her unstable drug level.
Her immigration concerns also became part of the dosing advice. Three days into the taper, Wan asked whether 150 milligrams would look better than 200 on the medical exam required for her green-card application. ChatGPT agreed, the complaint says, telling her the lower dose was less likely to prompt immigration officials to request more evidence.
Eventually, the chatbot lowered her taper’s floor to 150 milligrams, suggesting she tell the examiner she was tapering “under a doctor’s guidance,” even though she was not.
Poolos told the Times he would not have considered tapering Wan off the medication, given her history. “No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”
Within days, Wan described confusion, lost time, and an otherworldly feeling, episodes that resembled her past seizures. ChatGPT framed each one as her brain readjusting. The Times counted at least 158 times she voiced worry about the taper. After one episode, she wrote that she felt “a little scared.” The bot replied, “You have absolutely no need to worry.”
At 8:01 p.m. PT on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan sent her final message, asking whether the pain in her head was similar to pain from a fever. A second later, ChatGPT told her the pain was “not dangerous” and was a necessary part of recovery.
The chatbot’s final response offered to draw her a chart comparing withdrawal pain with fever pain and told her, “This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself.”
Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her, and they found her body three days later. A postmortem test found that her lamotrigine level was 0.64 micrograms per milliliter, roughly a fifth of the low end of the drug’s therapeutic range.
The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content. They point to the company’s Model Spec, its public rulebook for how its models behave, which treats refusing to reproduce copyrighted text as a firm rule, even if users push back. Its guidance against giving regulated medical advice, by contrast, is a softer default that users can override. The suit argues medication advice deserved the same hard limit.
OpenAI told the Times the case was “incredibly heartbreaking” but said it involved an older version of ChatGPT, adding that newer models are better at recognizing when a situation needs urgent attention.
Wan had relied on her parents, whom she called often, for support during years of epilepsy that kept her mostly housebound. In 2023, she started using ChatGPT for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits.
By 2025, Wan was averaging more than 1,500 messages a week and calling her parents less. “Sometimes when we chat, no matter what it’s about, I’ve started to see you...

title_en: This one missing feature from the Slate truck might be a dealbreaker for truck enthusiasts
title_fa: This one missing feature from the Slate truck might be a dealbreaker for truck enthusiasts
excerpt_en: The Slate Truck is known for offering hundreds of customization options, but one common truck option isn't available (yet.)
excerpt_fa: The Slate Truck is known for offering hundreds of customization options, but one common truck option isn't available (yet.)
content_en:
This one missing feature from the Slate truck might be a dealbreaker for truck enthusiasts
It's a pretty major limitation.
Slate is bringing something new to the EV truck market. The truck startup has quickly made a name for itself with its minimalist design, low price point and customization features. Playfully crowned the Blank Slate, the Michigan-based manufacturer's flagship truck does away with pesky features like speakers and automatic windows in favor of a $24,950 base price. But even with hundreds of add-ons and vinyl wraps, the build-your-own truck company is hoping that the biggest roadblock to getting you in an EV is the market's elevated prices.
Luckily, the company's minimalist approach doesn't apply to the truck's performance. With a 135 kW motor, the EV delivers 181 horsepower, 195 ft-lb of torque and 2,000 pounds of towing power. These metrics are in line with the hybrid Ford Maverick. And while its 205-mile range leaves something to be desired, the biggest concern for trucking purists may be the Slate truck's commitment to two-wheel drive.
Slate, which has pitched its truck more as an everyday vehicle than a heavy-duty towing machine, currently only offers rear-wheel drive. However, this may change with later models. According to an email posted to the Slate truck fan forum, "all-wheel drive is in the plans for a future version of Slate." According to the post, although such options won't be available at launch, Slate knows "how important it is for folks in snowier climates, on job sites, or looking for that extra traction."
Of course, such projections should be taken with a grain of salt. To date, Slate has yet to verify whether a different drivetrain is in the works. We've reached out to Slate for confirmation and will update the story accordingly. In the meantime, let's look at how Slate drivers can benefit from all-wheel drive, and why Slate has chosen not to offer it at this time.
Behind the drivetrain debate
The desire for four-wheel drive and all-wheel drive options is logical. Because these drive systems send power to each wheel, they can maximize control and improve traction when driving in uncertain conditions. So if you plan on camping in the woods, need to haul large payloads over unpaved roads or expect to be driving in slick conditions, a truck with 4x4 or all-wheel drive is worth considering.
But Slate's decision to use a rear two-wheel drivetrain is also sound. First and foremost is cost, as adding AWD or 4WD substantially raises a vehicle's price tag. Considering Slate's mission to deliver "the most affordable truck in America," using rear-wheel drive is an easy way to lower costs. Moreover, AWD and 4WD drivetrains typically increase maintenance costs. The extra energy expenditure of powering all four wheels can also decrease an EV's range, potentially exacerbating an already-acute challenge for Slate drivers. Rear-wheel drive also offers more towing capacity, adding to its case as a more efficient option for the EV.
Rear-wheel drive also better fits Slate's audience. Notably, the startup doesn't market its trucks as heavy-duty haulers or off-roading demons. Instead, Slate argues that its trucks are "built for everyday practicality," with the company stating that its drivetrain strikes a balance between battery range, towing performance, traction, stability and thermal limits.
These considerations are notable given the peculiarities of EV towing. Capable of generating max torque instantly, EV trucks are great for low-speed hauling. However, Slate's website notes that "sustained towing creates heat, and EVs need to protect motors, inverters, and battery systems from overload." Ultimately, your Slate truck can accomplish most daily needs and is ideal for "small trailers, motorcycles, yard equipment, kayaks, camping setups, and weekend utility jobs."
Getting a Slate
The EVs come in both truck and SUV styles. If you are looking to add a second row of seats, the SUVs come in squareback, fastback and open-air kits. Once you've chosen your body, you can cycle through over 200 accessories and a phantasmagoria of vinyl wraps. You can also choose from several unique starter packs and collaborations. Interestingly, buyers don't need to select all their accessories and wraps at once. Slate's DIY approach is meant to keep things cheap and customizable, allowing your ride to evolve along with you.
Pre-orders are currently open, and the first deliveries are set for late 2026. Those willing to put down a $300 deposit can cement their spot in the next delivery window. As it stands, Slate states that new orders will likely begin to ship from its Warsaw, Indiana, factory as early as July 2027. Notably, buyers will also be charged a $1,450 destination fee, which covers transportation and delivery costs.
You can begin your Slate journey by visiting the startup's website. There, you can begin designing your dream truck from the ground up via the startup's design tool. Customizing your electric truck is fun, easy and highly addictive. For more information on Slate's novel EV, you can read my colleague Tim's insightful review after a day behind the wheel. If you still have questions, Slate's helpful FAQ page is likely to cover them, with answers ranging from how to install your latest accessories to how many dachshunds can fit in the cargo bed (spoiler: 30).

title_en: Discord public server messages may be soon searchable on Google, but you can opt out
title_fa: Discord public server messages may be soon searchable on Google, but you can opt out
excerpt_en: The platform's Discoverable Servers are about to get a lot more discoverable.
excerpt_fa: The platform's Discoverable Servers are about to get a lot more discoverable.
content_en:
Discord public server messages may be soon searchable on Google, but you can opt out
The platform’s Discoverable Servers are about to get a lot more discoverable.
Discord is making a policy change that will further increase the visibility of conversations on its largest public servers. On November 16, the platform's Discoverable Servers will all be getting Server Web Pages. These hubs will display some basic information about the server, including a description and summaries of discussions happening on their public channels. By mid-December, Discord said that messages on posted to those channels could start appearing word-for-word on both the Server Web Pages and in search engine results. Neither the channel summaries nor the individual channel messages will display the poster's username or avatar.
The reason Discord gave for the change is to make it easier for information from these communities to be surfaced in web searches. In other words, you might start seeing Discord pages and messages the same way you'd find a Reddit thread among search hits.
This change is limited to Discoverable Servers, the large communities of at least 1,000 members where no invitation is required to join. Private servers, DMs and Group DMs will remain private. But considering Discord just weathered blowback over its implementation of age verification policies, this decision could raise new questions around how the platform handles privacy concerns.
Server admins for those Discoverable Servers can take action starting now to opt-out channels from being included in their eventual web presence. And individual users can also choose to keep their Discoverable Server posts from being indexed via the Data and Privacy section of Discord's User Settings. In select markets — the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia and South Korea — channel messages will be off by default to honor local regulations, so for those regions users will have to manually opt in to the feature. Teen Discord users are also excluded and do not have the option to turn on channel messages until they are of adult age.

title_fa: How to change and customize your Android Auto display
excerpt_en: Tailor your tech to fit your daily drive seamlessly.
excerpt_fa: Tailor your tech to fit your daily drive seamlessly.
content_en:
How to change and customize your Android Auto display
Tailor your tech to fit your daily drive seamlessly.
Most drivers stick with Android Auto's default setup from the moment they connect their phone, never realizing just how much of the display can be reshaped to fit their habits. From rearranging your layout to building one-tap shortcuts, Android Auto gives you more control over your dashboard than its stock appearance suggests.
The display of Android Auto can be tailored to match your driving habits perfectly without even having to dip into any hidden menus. With options to rearrange icons, create custom shortcuts and adjust visual elements, it allows you to design a dashboard that feels intuitive and personal. Whether you prioritize navigation, music or communication, every feature can be optimized for seamless access, making your driving experience smoother and more efficient.
Every adjustment takes just a minute or two, but together they add up to a noticeably smoother, safer and more personal driving experience. Whether you're commuting daily or taking the occasional road trip, these settings are worth exploring.
Make Android Auto yours
Let's start by customizing the launcher. Most of the customization can be done from your phone while just a few tweaks can be done from the car screen. Go to Settings > Connected devices > Android Auto (or just search for Android Auto in Settings) and tap Customize launcher. From there, you can choose which apps to hide and which to show, and you can even drag their names to rearrange the order they show up on the screen. You can, for example, make the Spotify app easier to reach and bump down less used apps like the Reminder app or the Weather app. You should also know that hiding an app only removes it from the car screen, it doesn't uninstall it from your phone.
The same Customize launcher page has an option to add a shortcut that calls a contact or triggers an Assistant action. These then appear in the car launcher alongside your apps. One I find super handy is to have Gemini navigate me home, check the ETA and text my husband to tell them I'm on the way and should arrive by a certain time. I can trigger this by pressing the button on the Android Auto launcher or by using a voice command. I've also told Gemini my best friend's name and can just say "Hey Google, call my bestie" and I won't have to look through contacts at a red light.
Change the layout and wallpaper
Android Auto's many settings let you make even more decisions on how the screen looks in your car. If you scroll down to Change layout you can choose whether the map or your media player sits closer to the driver. This matters quite a bit if you rely heavily on turn-by-turn navigation, keeping the map within easy glance distance and reducing how long your eyes leave the road. If you prioritize podcasts and playlists on the go, the opposite setup may be preferred. Make sure to test both configurations against your car's screen size because wider displays handle split layouts better than smaller ones.
If you're tired of your Android Auto screen looking boring, there's a way to fix that too. Some years ago, you could pick one of many wallpapers Google had preloaded. Nowadays, you can make your car's infotainment screen display your phone's wallpaper. You'll need to make this choice from your car, though, because you can't adjust it from your phone. Launch Android Auto, go to Settings and flip the toggle for the Use Phone's Wallpaper feature. Immediately, the background will mimic that of your phone. It's not much, but it's better than a blank space.
The Android Auto settings also make it possible to force day or night mode on your map. By default, the system automatically toggles between them based on ambient light and time of day. You can do this from the Maps section in the Android Auto settings. Also, if you no longer want Android Auto to automatically start media playback when you start driving, you can flip the switch on that feature too (under the Startup section).
None of these fixes take more than a couple of minutes individually, but together they reshape how Android Auto functions. Set up some widgets, adjust the layout, mirror your wallpaper and you get a way more pleasant driving experience.

title_en: The data center boom has an upside: innovation for the US grid
title_fa: The data center boom has an upside: innovation for the US grid
excerpt_en: As the AI boom stresses the existing power grid, all sorts of new opportunities for grid modernization are also emerging as a result, industry insiders say.
excerpt_fa: As the AI boom stresses the existing power grid, all sorts of new opportunities for grid modernization are also emerging as a result, industry insiders say.
content_en:
The AI boom has led to a gargantuan surge in energy demand across the country. Critics say this upswell in connections is enacting a stress test on America’s aging grid infrastructure. Worries abound that, in the short term, the energy crunch could lead to surging electrical bills and, in the long term, may eventually lead to outages or other technical problems.
At TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this month, industry insiders tempered much of this criticism with optimism about how the flood of new energy connections could actually be opening the door for grid modernization. Apoorv Bhargava, founder and CEO of WeaveGrid, Tim Heidel, CEO of Veir, and Kristin Eberhard, VP of policy at Rewiring America, said that though the grid faces new challenges, there are also plenty of new opportunities as well.
“It’s a very different electric grid, right?” said Bhargava. “We’re dealing with a ton of new variables, including renewable energy. We’re dealing with a ton of new load in the form of electric vehicles and data centers and heat pumps, and the ability to manage and orchestrate is fundamentally what utilities are now grappling with.”
While all of those new connections are driving an ever larger amount of stress to the grid, Bhargava’s company hopes to provide the kind of load orchestration and management that helps utilities maximize the potential of the current system. WeaveGrid’s software can help organizations efficiently deploy energy while also optimizing connections to reduce utility payers’ bills, the founder said.
Heidel, on the other hand, runs a company that is working to build out and expand the physical infrastructure of the grid, while also making it run much more efficiently. Veir sells superconductive power lines that promise to transfer energy at a much more efficient rate than traditional ones. Veir’s cables can carry power five times farther than traditional cables while also requiring 20 times less space, the company has said. Earlier this month the startup raised $110 million in a Series C funding round.
“The scale of the investment in AI infrastructure is driving a tremendous amount of innovation,” said Heidel. “There’s a ton of new technologies that are coming off the shelves and starting to get to scale that, pulled together, can actually really make sure that data centers are the best community neighbors and citizens they can possibly be.”
He added: “I think that we really need to look at ways that we can really adopt all of that as fast as possible to ease this next stage of growth.”
Eberhard, whose organization advocates for household electrification, also said that while the surge in data center energy demand has spurred a new urgency to the modernization cause, it has also created an environment where industries are ready to try new things.
“I feel like this era of AI and load growth is a very improv era,” Eberhard said. “There’s a lot of yes-and-ing going on. So yes, we need more transmission lines. Yes, we need more centralized power plants, and we also need to make sure that we’re taking advantage of all this other stuff that we had previously been leaving on the table when we didn’t have this urgency of the AI demand.”

title_en: Here’s why the iPhone Duo’s hinge could be cracking the screen
title_fa: Here’s why the iPhone Duo’s hinge could be cracking the screen
excerpt_en: Within hours of the iPhone Duo launch last Friday, people reported that the inner screen on some brand new foldable phones was already broken. The issue was similar across many photos shared on social media: some kind of issue or crack would appear in the middle of the screen...
excerpt_fa: Within hours of the iPhone Duo launch last Friday, people reported that the inner screen on some brand new foldable phones was already broken. The issue was similar across many photos shared on social media: some kind of issue or crack would appear in the middle of the screen...
content_en:
Within hours of the iPhone Duo launch last Friday, people reported that the inner screen on some brand new foldable phones was already broken. The issue was similar across many photos shared on social media: some kind of issue or crack would appear in the middle of the screen above the hinge, with lines appearing on the right side of the display. On Monday, Apple acknowledged an “issue” and said it’s replacing damaged units, without going into much detail about how many broken phones have been reported so far.
Here’s why the iPhone Duo’s hinge could be cracking the screen
Inside Apple’s first folding iPhone, contact with the delicate inner screen could cause a stress ‘hotspot.’
Inside Apple’s first folding iPhone, contact with the delicate inner screen could cause a stress ‘hotspot.’
So what’s actually going on?
Shahram Mokhtari, the lead teardown technician at iFixit, has actually taken apart the iPhone Duo and has a pretty good idea about the potential cause, telling The Verge that it’s due to an issue along the hinge, where a series of gears, springs, and joints work together to let the device close flat, while also trying to avoid creating a deeper crease by giving that screen space to bend more gently inside while it’s closed.
At the troublesome spot, it appears that the flexible inner screen is pushing up against a part of the hinge. That inner screen is already “extremely sensitive,” he says — if you took a pick or a sharp tool and poked at the edges of the screen, “you’re going to break that screen.” If you look at the pictures of damaged Duos on social media, there’s often a black spot where the damage is focused on the display, and that’s where the metal is hitting the screen, Mokhtari says.
You can see a visual representation of what Mokhtari is talking about in iFixit’s written and video Duo teardowns, which reveal where the hinge transitions, as the center hinge support makes space for a crossing flex cable, creating several edges that could ultimately be the culprit. The damage iFixit has been seeing is at a point where the center support bar might not always drop down far enough while the screen folds, possibly creating a stress “hot spot” between the flat bar and the bent screen inside a closed iPhone Duo.
At least one user with a broken Duo screen said they “felt something around the internal hinge” while showing it to a friend, kept opening it, and heard an “audible crack,” with the screen breaking. YouTuber CuriousHagi, who covered a Duo with dirt as part of a strenuous durability test, captured something similar on video, and the screen break appears in a similar spot. In a teardown video, CuriousHagi found that a part of the hinge that connects to the central bar had snapped.
Apple says the issue affects a “small number” of Duo units, and Mokhtari says that “In terms of numbers, we don’t know. Apple definitely has all the data here. And I suspect they know more than they’re telling us as well.” But he notes that because foldable screens are so delicate, a “certain number” of them will fail, as will a number of the hinges because they’re also “extremely complicated and delicate.” And while Apple isn’t recalling the Duos, “If three months from now, we’re still seeing the same kind of failure, then it’s a more widespread problem, and that might lead to a recall,” Mokhtari says.
Mokhtari points out that since this is the first generation of the iPhone Duo, it’s the first time Apple’s engineers are getting data on the hinge, and he says that “I guarantee you” Apple will redesign what’s at fault here for its next-generation foldable. He also notes that, generally speaking, “the phones do seem to be in people’s hands and people are using them, and they’re not running into any issues whatsoever.”

title_en: The best ways to tell if someone is using AI glasses
title_fa: The best ways to tell if someone is using AI glasses
excerpt_en: While it can be jarring to discover that your companion is using AI glasses, there are some steps you can take to recognize them ASAP.
excerpt_fa: While it can be jarring to discover that your companion is using AI glasses, there are some steps you can take to recognize them ASAP.
content_en:
The best ways to tell if someone is using AI glasses
Smart glasses are making unwanted surveillance all too easy, but you're far from powerless against this covert tech.
Smart glasses might be the next big trend in consumer tech, as there's certainly real demand for these gadget-intensive pieces of eyewear. However, there are very legitimate concerns about how these glasses can be used for stalking or other shady activity, especially as the prevalence of public recording comes more and more under scrutiny. If you share those concerns, you might want to keep an eye out for some tell-tale signs of AI glasses.
Of course, it could be a little rude to go around asking random people if they're wearing AI glasses when you're going off a gut instinct. Luckily, most (albeit not all) smart glasses brands have built-in signs of use. If you can't rely on those giveaways, there are some solid-enough reasons for you to be suspicious.
How to recognize whether someone's using smart glasses
Smart glasses are actually pretty easy to recognize at a glance, as their tech-riddled innards often require thick frames, particularly around the temples and the outer sides of the lenses (although this admittedly isn't always the case). That second area is typically where camera lenses are located, while any giveaway ports or grilles might be further back on the design. Most smart glasses also have an indicator light that turns on when they're filming; if you suspect you're being filmed via smart glasses, look for a small LED light.
However, there are reports of a variety of low-cost dupe glasses being sold on sites such as TikTok Shop and Temu that don't have a recording light (as well as audio-first glasses that don't have cameras, such as the Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses), so you'll need to look closer at the aforementioned physical traits. You can also check whether someone you suspect is recording is quickly pressing the temples of their glasses, pausing every now and then to zone out (as if to read text on their glasses' display), or whispering quiet voice commands to themselves. These could be signs of someone interacting with their smart glasses, though there is a small chance they are all completely unrelated.
The apps that can warn you about smart glasses
One of the most recent developments in the arms race against this tech is the arrival of apps that can warn you if smart glasses are nearby. The likes of Nearby Glasses and ZuckOff scan for nearby Bluetooth devices and the identifiers often associated with AI glasses. Admittedly, both of these apps aren't completely reliable. For one thing, there's a chance that anyone wearing smart glasses nearby has turned off their Bluetooth. There's also a risk of false positives. However, both can serve as your first line of defense against nearby smart glasses.
Just because you have a strong suspicion that there are AI glasses nearby, though, doesn't mean you should jump immediately to a confrontation. The best thing to do if someone near you is stirring your suspicions is to move away from the individual and speak to the authorities if you're being followed. If you're hosting a meeting or event that demands a level of confidentiality, it may be worth making a neutral statement about smart glasses not being permitted. In either case, if you need to speak with a stranger about whether they're recording you without your knowledge, do so calmly in a public environment.

title_en: Guidewire buys Hyperexponential for $1.7B in cash
title_fa: Guidewire buys Hyperexponential for $1.7B in cash
excerpt_en: The deal, expected to close sometime next year, is to help bring AI agents to work alongside humans to underwrite, analyze, and price decisions.
excerpt_fa: The deal, expected to close sometime next year, is to help bring AI agents to work alongside humans to underwrite, analyze, and price decisions.
content_en:
Insurance tech company Guidewire announced Tuesday the acquisition of the agentic underwriting insurance company Hyperexponential for $1.7 billion in cash.
The deal, expected to close sometime next year, is to help bring AI agents to work alongside humans to underwrite, analyze, and price decisions. The deal is worth around $2 billion in total, with $400 million in additional capital reserved if certain revenue targets are hit.
Backed by Andreessen Horowitz and Battery Ventures, Hyperexponential was founded in 2017 and has raised nearly $90 million to date, according to PitchBook. So this marks a significant return for investors. The U.K.-based AI startup says nearly 600 insurers across 40 different countries use its software.

title_en: From 8VC to Benchmark, here’s what’s hiding in October SEC filings
title_fa: From 8VC to Benchmark, here’s what’s hiding in October SEC filings
excerpt_en: A whole crop of venture capital firms are raising significant new funds.
excerpt_fa: A whole crop of venture capital firms are raising significant new funds.
content_en:
October was a big month for venture funds, per SEC filings. The filings show that established names are currently commanding top dollar from LPs, especially with a specialized focus. Here are some of the most notable ones we found that haven’t been meaningfully announced or have seen important updates.
For one, Trust Ventures filed Monday to raise a $400 million Fund V. The Austin-based firm was founded in 2017 by Salen Churi to back founders building in highly regulated industries. Koch Disruptive Technologies notably backed the firm’s debut fund back in 2018. It previously sought to raise a $225 million Fund IV in 2023, though it’s unclear if or when that fund closed. Deep tech fund Interlagos Capital is also raising a $400 million Fund II.
Elsewhere, Victor Lazarte and Kris Fredrickson, two former Benchmark VCs, have raised $1.252 billion for their debut AI fund called Diffusion ONE. Forbes previously reported back in May that the two had teamed up (after raising smaller funds of their own) to launch this fund with a target of $800 million, meaning it’s far surpassed that original target. The firm has already cut big checks since its debut, including co-leading Harvey’s $550 million Series H with Lightspeed Ventures and taking part in Etched’s $300 million Series C, announced in July.
Speaking of Benchmark, the firm filed what looks like four new partner-only funds, called Benchmark Partners Founders’ Fund T1, Benchmark Partners Founders’ Fund 2, Benchmark Partners Founders’ Fund 2-A, and Benchmark Partners Founders’ Fund T1-A, seeking to raise $220 million, $132 million, $4.5 million, and $7.5 million, respectively. Jack Altman, who recently left his own firm to join Benchmark, is listed in each filing.
Meanwhile, Joe Lonsdale’s 8VC also seems to be seeking to raise new vehicles — including a $400 million fund called 8VC DSS III; a $30.35 million fund called 8VC COSC; a $20.35 million 8VC BRSC fund; and a fund called 8VC AI Fund XI, which has already raised $13.5 million, including from 8VC itself. This follows the July news that 8VC raised $1.5 billion for Fund VII.

title_en: What are wrong number text scams, and how can you avoid them?
title_fa: What are wrong number text scams, and how can you avoid them?
excerpt_en: It's not an honest mistake; it's the start of an attack on your wallet.
excerpt_fa: It's not an honest mistake; it's the start of an attack on your wallet.
content_en:
What are wrong number text scams, and how can you avoid them?
It’s not an honest mistake; it’s the start of an attack on your wallet.
There's a good chance you've gotten a message from a "wrong number" at least once. These follow a familiar pattern: a random number asks a question addressed to a name that's not yours, so you politely respond and say they have the wrong number. Instead of acknowledging this and moving on, they thank you for being so kind and ask if you want to be friends.
While the other person might claim that it's "fate" you met like this, a terrible fate awaits if you continue talking to them. It's the start of a scam, not a friendly person looking for conversation — one of many ways crooks try to take advantage of you being kind.
How a wrong number scam develops
If you continue talking to a "new friend" who contacts you this way via standard text message, they'll eventually ask you to move to another messaging app like WhatsApp or Telegram. There are several reasons for this, including centralizing their communication, avoiding fees associated with SMS in other countries and splitting duties among their teams. Once you connect with a person on a web-based messaging app, they'll begin to develop a "friendship" with you, checking in throughout the day.
These greetings often start with relatively innocuous questions, like asking whether you've eaten. In many cases, conversations take on a "romantic" element. These people will pretend to share in personal matters you mention to them, like the loss of a spouse. The scammers like to send pictures, almost always claiming to be Asian women living in major US cities as entrepreneurs.
They'll often hint at being wealthy by showing luxury purses or mentioning that they just got done golfing at a fancy course. After a short period of "normal" conversation, the scammer will bring up some mention of investing in cryptocurrencies, often mentioning that some member of their family has made a ton of money by doing so.
From here, they'll goad you into signing up for a (legitimate) crypto exchange platform, if you don't already use one. They'll show you screenshots of the gains you can supposedly earn by investing in their platform and pressure you to take advantage.
What happens if you try to withdraw
If you go along with their asks, the scammer will guide you through buying real crypto and then "investing" it in a platform they claim they've made huge returns on. In reality, you're sending money to their crypto wallet that you'll never see again. But a single transaction won't be the end. They'll show you fake "growth" results and encourage you to "invest" more. They'll go even further, too, often urging you to take out a loan or borrow cash from friends to put even more in.
Typically, the scam goes on until you want to get your money out. If you try to withdraw a lot, they might say there are taxes and fees to pay — which you can conveniently only cover with new deposits, not the money already supposedly in the account. Once they don't think they can deceive you any longer, they may send you a nasty message blaming you for losing your money or making fun of you for falling for the scam. Then they cut off all contact, and there's very little chance of getting your money back given the nature of crypto.
While it's an awful feeling to realize you've been fleeced, these con artists might not even stop there. Earlier this week, I got a random Telegram message from someone claiming to be a victim of these scams. They mentioned that they had been given a "list" of other victims and that one of them knew a "hacker" who might be able to help folks recover their money — with no cost unless it's successful.
As you probably guessed, this is a follow-up scam. Anyone contacting you who claims to be a lawyer, detective or similar is trying to take further advantage of you and steal even more of your money. You're more likely to be targeted if you post about being a victim online, though apparently these scams are common enough now that randomly messaging people about recovery is a viable strategy.
Staying safe from these scammers
This scam might sound silly if you're careful about online security and generally refrain from engaging with messages from unknown numbers. Even when I've intentionally engaged with these scammers to better understand how they work, I found their messages incredibly bland and annoying. However, they're depressingly effective.
Americans lost over $1 billion to romance scams in 2025, so con artists aren't going to stop anytime soon. And the people who send money aren't the only victims — many of these scam organizations operate by tricking people with fake job ads, then capturing them and forcing them to work under threat of extreme punishment. It's an upsetting situation from every angle.
The best advice to stay safe, which you should share with those in your life who aren't as tech-savvy, is to be skeptical of everything online. Assume everything is phony until you have clear proof that it's legitimate. Recognizing the patterns of common scams is also vital; these almost always play out in the same way, so knowing what's coming before it develops gives you the upper hand.
For instance, it's worth considering anything involving gift cards, and virtually everything with crypto, a scam. Gift cards are a favorite for fraudsters because they're gone instantly and can't be traced. Crypto obviously has legitimate uses, but it's utilized by bad actors against people who don't know any better.
It's also a good idea to limit the amount of information you share about yourself online, especially in public forums. Anything people know about you is something they can exploit to falsely connect with you. Also consider switching away from Telegram to another messaging platform. While I used to get most "wrong numbers" via SMS, they usually come via Telegram now — and might even start with a voice message, which could trick someone more...

title_en: GM is embracing hybrids now
title_fa: GM is embracing hybrids now
excerpt_en: GM eschewed hybrids in favor of battery-electric vehicles. Now it's gearing up to offer hybrid versions of its SUVs.
excerpt_fa: GM eschewed hybrids in favor of battery-electric vehicles. Now it's gearing up to offer hybrid versions of its SUVs.
content_en:
General Motors plans to invest in its Lansing Delta Township Assembly plant to handle future production of hybrid-electric vehicles, the latest move by the U.S. automaker to claw back market share by appealing to the shifting tastes of consumers.
The company said on Tuesday that it plans to invest more than $2 billion over the next several years in the broader Lansing region, an amount that includes $1.25 billion to prepare the assembly plant for “future vehicle production.”
The company said it is working with the U.S. Department of Energy to restructure a previously awarded Domestic Manufacturing Conversion Grant and direct those funds to future hybrid production at the Lansing factory. The company was awarded $500 million under the Biden administration to support converting a different factory in Lansing to produce electric vehicles, including hybrid, battery-electric, plug-in electric hybrid, and hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles. Those funds were never released, according to GM.
Today, GM assembles the gas-powered Buick Enclave, Chevrolet Traverse, and GMC Acadia at the Lansing Delta Township factory, which produced a record 291,000 vehicles in 2025.
GM didn’t provide specifics on when it would begin producing and selling hybrid vehicles. But insiders told TechCrunch to expect hybrids across multiple brands rather than a single vehicle line. A Reuters report, citing anonymous sources, said the company plans to build hybrid versions of the Chevrolet Traverse, Buick Enclave, and GMC Acadia at the factory.
Hybrids have become increasingly popular, thanks in part to rising gas prices. Customers also have more choices than ever before, with most automakers offering a range of hybrid and plug-in hybrid models. Toyota is the U.S. market leader in hybrid sales, followed by Honda. Ford has also gained considerable market share in hybrid sales in the past two years, selling some 228,000 hybrids in 2025.
But GM has been slow to adopt hybrids. Until recently, the company’s only electric-hybrid vehicle was the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, which launched as a 2024 model. (GM sold 2,444 of those vehicles last year.) The E-Ray has since been discontinued; GM began deliveries of the hybrid Corvette ZR1X in March and next year will launch a hybrid Corvette Grand Sport X.
GM eschewed hybrids in favor of battery-electric vehicles. The automaker invested billions of dollars to shift its gas-powered portfolio to an all-electric one. That strategy has changed under the Trump administration with the end of the federal EV tax credit and slower-than-expected demand. GM hasn’t abandoned EVs completely, though it has seen EV sales fall year-over-year. The company still sells numerous battery-electric vehicles across its brands, including the Chevrolet Equinox EV, Blazer EV, and Cadillac Escalade IQ.
GM said Tuesday it will share specific details on its hybrid vehicle production plans closer to launch.

title_en: Bank of America kindly asks that you don’t share your banking password with your AI assistant
title_fa: Bank of America kindly asks that you don’t share your banking password with your AI assistant
excerpt_en: The banking giant reminds customers that "you're responsible for activity" resulting from your AI agents' access.
excerpt_fa: The banking giant reminds customers that "you're responsible for activity" resulting from your AI agents' access.
content_en:
Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.
In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.”
You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular. Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account.
This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money. As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.
A spokesperson for Bank of America confirmed the authenticity of the bank’s email that was posted to social media. But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you. Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”
(via Bryan Toporek)

title_en: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
title_fa: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
excerpt_en: Here's a clear explanation of Anthropic's incredibly complex governance structure.
excerpt_fa: Here's a clear explanation of Anthropic's incredibly complex governance structure.
content_en:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.
Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.
First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.
Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board.
Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.
Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.
Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.
Here’s what all that looks like:
The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.
At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.
The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.
If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.

Even Grok isn't sure.

People are starting to see a brief animation of an arm taking over the post composer in the X app. The arm appears only briefly and points at the "promote" button, according to multiple posts and screenshots from users.
The change doesn't seem to have hit all accounts just yet. The "promote" button appears in the composer view for accounts with a paid subscription to X Premium. The randomness of the new animation, though, is confusing X users. Is the company that desperate for promoted posts? Is it a prank? X hasn't publicly weighed in.
Here I am wanting to post my typical GM post and I get spooked by this animated hand pointing at promoting it... is this some sort of Halloween joke or we going to be forced to ignore it every time we want to post something from here on?
(Try it! That hand just pops out of... pic.twitter.com/KbaVypGqp7
— MartaTrades (@AureaLuma) October 27, 2026
Every PM has basically wanted to point at the button they want users to click, but instead spends time designing subtle nudges.
Kudos to X for just shipping this arm. pic.twitter.com/Fo1PAOzbLq
— aneri (@0xaneri) October 27, 2026
I was about to post a photo of my new iPhone Duo on X and this giant arm came out pointing at the "promote" button — what's this all about? pic.twitter.com/mcKPj3ZdI9
— Casey (@casey_lau) October 27, 2026
The appearance of the mystery arm also roughly coincides with X hiring Peter Sellis, its new head of product. Sellis, who is taking over for Nikita Bier, previously held similar roles at Discord and Snap. And, like Bier, he's known as something of a shitposter. In his post announcing he was joining X, he said that "it's time to make shitposting multiplanetary." It's not clear how an unexplained arm would contribute to that goal, but we do know Elon Musk is a fan of a dramatic, if cringey, entrance.
So while there's been some speculation the hand could be the work of Sellis, he hasn't publicly commented on the arm either. It could also simply be a Halloween-related prank, as Grok has speculated.
"That hand is real—not a glitch or pure Easter egg," Grok told one user. "Lots of users got the same jumpscare today. No official word if it's intentional design or Halloween timing." The bot gave similar replies to other perplexed users.
A representative for X didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the hand.

title_en: iPhone 18e reportedly comes with 2nm A20 chip and 60Hz screen
title_fa: iPhone 18e reportedly comes with 2nm A20 chip and 60Hz screen
excerpt_en: The leaks suggest the front camera could also see a boost.
excerpt_fa: The leaks suggest the front camera could also see a boost.
content_en:
iPhone 18e reportedly comes with 2nm A20 chip and 60Hz screen
The leaks suggest the front camera could also see a boost.
Apple is still in the throes of all its fall hardware announcements, but there are already hints of what might be coming from the company in spring. New leaks from social media posts by Digital Chat Station on Weibo suggest what the next wave of specs for the iPhone 18e will be. As reported by 9to5Mac, the leaker says the next iteration of the entry-level smartphone will have an A20 chip, which to date has not appeared except as a Pro model. The iPhone 17e had a 3nm A19 chip, so the swap to a 2nm A20, even one that isn't at Pro level, could offer some notable performance upgrades.
The post also suggests that the 18e will have a 48MP single rear camera, while the front camera "may be upgraded to 24MP." The other leaked specs fall in line with what the 17e had on offer, claiming the 18e will offer a 60Hz refresh rate on a 6.12-inch OLED screen. There are no hints about price, which should be particularly interesting given the continued high costs of components. Apple hasn't been immune to the impact of RAMaggedon; the company raised prices for large chunks of its product lineup in June and September.
An iPhone 18e will likely be announced in the spring, alongside a baseline iPhone 18 and a rumored second generation of the iPhone Air.
