The company certainly seems to have a lot of money for large-scale AI construction projects, but not too much for its human employees. It has been laying people off left and right. The Xbox division just got slammed with thousands of layoffs, and other departments have also suffered.
It is worth reiterating that this is a voluntary buyout program. That 60,000 number sounds huge, and it is, but we don't know how many people will accept the terms. Microsoft did something similar earlier this year and only 30 percent of eligible workers signed on the dotted line.

Last week, I sank into my living room couch and watched a bedraggled, nihilistic Matthew McConaughey take a drag of a cigarette in season 1 of True Detective. “You know, someone once told me time is a flat circle. Everything we’ve done, or will do, we’re gonna do over and over and over again.” I assume most people aren’t thinking about fitness trackers or gadgets while watching that scene. But in that moment, I couldn’t help but think about the Fitbit Edge on my wrist.
Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
The simple $180 tracker is a sleek return to Fitbit’s roots, albeit with a little extra AI flair.
Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
The simple $180 tracker is a sleek return to Fitbit’s roots, albeit with a little extra AI flair.
The $179.99 Edge is a modernized version of the 2014-to-2020 era of fitness bands — your Charges, your Altas, your Inspires. If you’ve ever owned one, you already know the vast majority of what the Edge is like. It’s lightweight. You swipe on a small display that shows you basic health and fitness metrics. It lasts for about a week on a charge — though that shrunk down to about a day and a half with the always-on display enabled. It’s a device that isn’t trying to be much more than what it is.
Fitbit Edge
The Good
- Easy to wear
- Long battery life
- Sleeker look
- Improved automatic activity tracking
- Very comfy
- Physical side button!
- Works on iOS and Android
The Bad
- Kinda expensive for what it is
- The alternative straps are really expensive
- No contactless payments
- Some of you will hate the bezels
The difference is that the Edge feels more refined on the wrist. Where the Fitbit Charge 6’s display felt boxy, the Edge is fully rounded, giving it a softer vibe. The straps are interchangeable, but with an easier button-release system. The metal link bracelet gives it a more jewelry-like feel, though it costs almost as much as the Edge itself at $150. I’m partial to the $60 magnetic strap, which mimics leather despite being made of silicone. The widgets borrow heavily from the Pixel Watch’s Material 3 Expressive redesign. Though to be clear, this is a proprietary Fitbit OS, not Wear OS. Some of the new watchfaces are elegant, though others highlight the Edge’s big black bezels. (Some things truly never change.)
Functionally, it’s also a step above the Fitbit Air. There’s built-in GPS for tracking walks and runs without your phone. You can have alarms, view notifications, and control music. You can’t take calls on the wrist — there are no microphones or speakers. Contactless payments are also a no-go. Andy Abramson, head of product at Google Health, says that’s because “less than one percent [of Charge 6 owners] used the feature” and that Google instead prioritized a “sleek design, altimeter, and weeklong battery.” That walks back some of the advancements that have come to the Charge lineup over the years, but if you want to put a silver lining on that, it narrows the Edge’s focus. This is a fitness tracker. There’s some glanceable information, but there’s absolutely no smartwatch creep here.
The big software change is the demise of the Fitbit app as we knew it. It’s Google Health now, with an AI coach if you pony up for the yearly subscription. (You get three months free with purchase; otherwise it’s $10 monthly.) I’ve written about the overall experience in my Fitbit Air review. The broad strokes are the same, though in the months since, Google has spent a lot of time tinkering with and iterating on it. Most notably, the company has beefed up automatic activity tracking.
To test this, I tracked a handful of runs on the Edge without officially starting an activity. I then compared that to one tracked by an Apple Watch Ultra 4 and my iPhone’s Runna app. I was surprised, but noticed limitations. For example, on a 2.4-mile run with a five-minute warmup walk and cooldown, the Edge correctly identified the exact moment my warmup transitioned into a legit run and then back into a walk. The estimated distance was also pretty decent at 2.55 miles. It wasn’t quite as good at gauging my running speed. It logged me as running a 10’49” mile pace, whereas my actual pace according to the Apple Watch and my phone was 11’38”. This pattern was fairly typical across my testing, so it’s more that this is a nifty way to still “get credit” if you forget to track an activity.
Otherwise, the AI coach is still a Chatty Cathy and requires some weekly hand-holding to get the most out of it. I’ll say it again: The Google Health app can feel cluttered, and I get tripped up looking for information that used to be easy to find, like past workouts. However, if you’re new to fitness and want guidance in creating and sticking to a custom AI-generated routine, this is still the best experience I’ve had so far. The bar is in hell, though, and beware what you initially share with the coach. I regret ever telling it I used to have shin splints, as it remains convinced my perfectly fine shins are in danger of disintegrating with every run.
I wish I could tell you about the Health Guardian features, which should let Fitbit Edge users see noninvasive insulin resistance and blood pressure trends. Alas, the way my testing schedule worked out, I have to wait until November 1st to get my initial results.
All in all, I enjoyed the Fitbit Edge as a low-key tracker. This will appeal to folks who just want the basics, but aren’t willing to commit to the screenless life. I’m thinking of the Vergecast listeners who occasionally write in, wondering what happened to simple fitness bands, tired of the smartwatch agenda that took over the past few years. The only gripe I really have is $179.99 feels a tad expensive for what you’re getting. Especially since the Fitbit Air is only $99, and for iPhone users, the Apple Watch SE 3 starts at $249. Brands like Xiaomi and Amazfit also offer much cheaper trackers with displays, even if they’re not quite as sleek on the wrist.

title_fa: Fitbit Edge review: Google strikes the right balance
excerpt_en: Want a beautiful tracker with a screen but don't want AI on your wrist? The Fitbit Edge is perfect for you.
excerpt_fa: Want a beautiful tracker with a screen but don't want AI on your wrist? The Fitbit Edge is perfect for you.
content_en:
Fitbit Edge review: Google strikes the right balance
Want a beautiful tracker with a screen but don’t want AI on your wrist? This is perfect for you.
In the ten years since I reviewed the original Fitbit Alta, I've noticed a pattern. Try as it might to create an activity tracker that looks attractive, Fitbit has never quite delivered. When the Fitbit Alta was launched in 2016, the company had been working with Tory Burch on accessories to make the device "super-chic." But with its rigid cuff-like band and generic appearance, the Alta didn't come off fashionable or pretty. It was just another fitness tracker in a smaller frame.
Fitbit later unveiled the Alta HR, which retained a similar appearance, and the more recent Luxe, with a shinier stainless steel case and softer, nicer-looking bands. And yet, despite the company's proud proclamation that the Luxe was one of its "most fashionable and comfortable devices yet," I found its small size more impressive than its style.
We live in a world of oblongs, and the Fitbit Edge is admittedly just a curvier and wider oblong than the Luxe and the Alta. Yet it packs quite a punch compared to those before it, thanks to a bright, navigable touchscreen, a more attractive array of straps and an updated feature set that makes the Edge feel as modern as it looks.
Design and display
A lot of what I like about the Fitbit Edge, especially compared to the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5 (and other modern smartwatches), lies entirely in its design. While I loved the simplicity of the Fitbit Air's screenless design, its lack of a display did have drawbacks. I always had to whip out my phone to start logging workouts, and it didn't have a readout of my heart rate for me to see if I should push harder or slow down. I'd have to keep my phone nearby so I could look at it for that data.
Meanwhile, though smartwatches like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Apple Watch have larger screens that enable all that, they tended to get in the way when I was doing pushups or moving planks, for instance. Thanks to its narrower shape, the Fitbit Edge stayed mostly tucked out of the way. I was pleasantly surprised to find that I could bend my wrist quite a generous angle without ever triggering its side button, and didn't have to turn it so its face was on the inside of my wrist. On wider-faced wearables like Apple, Pixel and Galaxy watches, their buttons would protrude too far and inadvertently get pushed.
Of course, similarly shaped activity trackers have existed for years as well, but what the Fitbit Edge brings is a shiny case, thinner bezels and a screen that elevates its functionality. I complained about the Luxe's display being small and hard to read. The Edge does not have that issue. Its display was consistently bright and easy to see in various lighting conditions, and it mostly recognized my taps and swipes promptly. Is it the most responsive touchscreen on a wearable? No — I occasionally found myself waiting for something to happen after I swiped to find a tile. But in those cases it was usually that the Edge was still in a sleep state. Most of the time when I was certain it was awake, the screen felt as responsive as the Pixel Watch's.
That's a significant step up from the lackluster and laggy displays on previous Fitbits, which took a lot of prodding to work. The physical button on the Edge's side is also easy to use, and frankly a relief when compared to the touch-sensitive faux button on the Inspire 3 and the haptic one on the Charge 6.
Speaking of the latter, in many ways the Fitbit Edge feels like its spiritual successor — a Charge 7, shall we say. The Edge has a similarly sized case, just a bit bigger and more rounded. Both share a lot of features, including Google Maps support and the ability to take ECG readings. But the Edge has a nicer, larger screen with adjustable brightness, an altimeter to measure elevation gain or steps climbed, GPS tracking for outdoor runs or walks and an IP68 certification for dust and water-resistance (in addition to the 5 ATM rating they both have). Not to mention, the Edge has a proper button and greater media playback support as well. The list of differences between the two models is long and complicated so I'll just point out that the Edge doesn't have NFC for contactless payments while the Charge 6 does. And finally, the new device costs about $20 more.
A word on Fitbit Edge straps (and the Fitbit Air's new metal mesh band)
One of the reasons the Edge is so appealing is its appearance, which is further enhanced by the bands you use with it. Google sent along two straps in addition to the silicone one that came in the box, and both of them really made the Edge look better. I also found it easy to swap out bands — just pushing down the catch on the device's underside and pulling away from the case would remove a strap. Connecting one was as simple as pushing it into the groove.
At first, I struggled to close the Magnet band that snapped together with, well, a magnetic clasp. But once I got the hang of it, I began to appreciate its appearance thanks to its narrow width and stainless steel lugs.
I also loved the Metal Links band that Google sent. The one I received was in gold and it matched my Edge's case so seamlessly that you wouldn't know it was a detachable accessory. My sweet naive gym friend told me they thought it looked like a Rolex. While I think the regulars at r/Rolex would scoff at that assessment, I agree that there is a premium vibe to the Metal Links band. That said, I have to warn you it costs $150, which is about the same price as a whole Fitbit Charge 6, and just $30 shy of the Fitbit Edge itself.
While we're on the topic, Google also sent me a sample of the new Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air, and I am a big fan of how it elevates the tracker's appearance. But I also have to point out that at $70, the Metal Mesh Band is just $30 shy of the Air's retail price. You can find cheaper options elsewhere, but I do think...

title_en: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
title_fa: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
excerpt_en: Anthropic’s S-1 shows more than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude Platform and a first-party app, a cross-selling playbook reminiscent of Amazon that’s making enterprise customers stickier.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic’s S-1 shows more than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude Platform and a first-party app, a cross-selling playbook reminiscent of Amazon that’s making enterprise customers stickier.
content_en:
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.
“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, reads.
As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upward of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.
Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.
Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.
“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.
The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce.
Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.
Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.
Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”
Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”
The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.
Customer concentration is another risk.
“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”
Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”
The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.
Customer concentration is another risk.
“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title_en: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
title_fa: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
excerpt_en: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
excerpt_fa: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
content_en:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday. In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing”.
Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.
SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.
The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.
Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”
The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.
The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business. SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.
Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.
The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.
While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.
Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.
“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

title_en: Here's how much it would cost to build a PC similar to the Xbox Series X
title_fa: Here's how much it would cost to build a PC similar to the Xbox Series X
excerpt_en: An Xbox Series X isn't cutting-edge tech anymore, but it's still costly to build a similar PC due to high part prices.
excerpt_fa: An Xbox Series X isn't cutting-edge tech anymore, but it's still costly to build a similar PC due to high part prices.
content_en:
Here's how much it would cost to build a PC similar to the Xbox Series X
Matching the $800 console will be costly with new parts, but you can save if you buy used.
When the Xbox Series X launched in November 2020 at what today sounds like a bargain price of $499.99, claims made the rounds online that $800 is all it'd take to build a PC to match it.
PCWorld put that to the test and came out at a total cost of $1,559, more than three times the original price of the console. Six years later, the Series X costs $799.99, and a matching PC still can't be built for that with new parts. Once you've added Windows and a controller, you're looking at a ballpark figure of $1,200. Even if you're only buying the main components used, you can expect to shell out roughly $730.
Xbox prices rose again on August 1 in the third US increase since the start of last year. To nobody's surprise, Microsoft pointed the finger at "the current components crisis," stating that memory and storage prices had risen by more than 2.5 times. Meanwhile, creating an equivalent PC has gotten cheaper because a six-year-old console doesn't take as much to keep up with. Plenty of parts at the cheaper end of the GPU market can do a job that needed more premium components in 2020.
The card in this build will cost you $330. Sure, you'll still pay more for the PC than the console, but the difference was roughly $1,060 in 2020 versus about $415 today.
The graphics cards that match a Series X
Inside the Series X is an eight-core AMD Zen 2 processor that runs at 3.8GHz. That's paired with an AMD graphics chip rated at 12 teraflops, a 1TB NVMe SSD and 16GB of memory shared between the system and graphics. There's no direct match to a PC card since that graphics chip was never sold as a PC part, but in 2020, Microsoft showed Digital Foundry a Gears 5 benchmark running about level with Nvidia's RTX 2080.
The RTX 2080 and 30-series cards that replaced it are now out of production, so we're basing our assessment on used prices. On resale marketplace Jawa, the RTX 2080 has sold for an average of $195 over the past 12 months, and the slightly slower RTX 2070 Super for $199. The newer RTX 3060 Ti sells for an average of $223, while AMD's RX 6700 XT averages about $260.
New cards in this class start around $310. On October 8, PC Gamer's price tracker had the RTX 5050 at $310 on sale, while Intel's 12GB Arc B580 was at $330. Tom's Hardware listed AMD's RX 7600 at $339. TechSpot, meanwhile, found the B580 within one percent of the RTX 4060 at 1080p across 50 games and 5 percent ahead at 1440p, though the 3060 Ti is 12 percent faster than the 4060 at 1080p.
Nvidia's RTX 4060 has almost disappeared from new stock, with Tom's Hardware's cheapest listing at $530 versus a roughly $261 average on Jawa. An RTX 5060 costs $439, which is up from $359 in mid-August.
Where's the rest of the money going?
A new build around the Arc B580 needs:
-
An eight-core Ryzen 7 5700X at $209
-
A $25 cooler (because the chip doesn't include one)
-
A $70 B550 motherboard,
-
16GB of DDR4 at $104,
-
A 1TB SSD at $149,
-
A $60 power supply, and
-
A $65 case.
That's $1,012 with the graphics card, so a $1,000 budget covers the parts, but Windows 11 Home adds $139 and an Xbox controller $65. PCWorld paid $64 for 16GB of RAM in 2020, but that ain't happening in 2026. Per Tom's Hardware, a 32GB DDR4 kit that cost $48 a year earlier was about $200 in July. Newer DDR5 prices are a far worse story, setting buyers back around $249 for 16GB. That's why we've settled on AMD's older AM4 platform for this build.
Forking out for a used processor, motherboard, memory and graphics card brings the parts bill to about $730. A Ryzen 7 3700X, the eight-core Zen 2 chip PCWorld used in its 2020 example build, fetches an average price of $91 on Jawa, a B450 motherboard $49 and a used 16GB DDR4 kit is about $70 on eBay. The remainder of the price is the $223 RTX 3060 Ti plus the same new SSD, power supply, case and cooler. Sellers are asking for more than those 12-month averages at the time of writing: Jawa's current average price for the 3060 Ti is around $284, so $800 is a more realistic number. Windows and a controller would then push the build past $900.
To cut costs a bit, you could get a cheaper third-party wired controller, and you might already have a Windows license on a current PC you could transfer.
Caveat emptor
PCWorld warned in September that those looking in the used market should be cautious, as it includes cards worn down by crypto mining, "untested" parts and listings embellished with AI-generated photos. Some sellers and manufacturers have outright refused returns on dead graphics cards. Meanwhile, Microsoft sells a Certified Refurbished Series X for $649.99, which undercuts the used PC and includes the 4K Blu-ray drive none of these builds have. If you're solely interested in Series X performance, buy the console.
However, an Xbox Series X obviously can't moonlight as a PC. It does have Developer Mode, but that's for testing apps and can't run retail games, so the extra few hundred dollars for a Series X-esque build only makes sense if you'll use the PC as one. Microsoft has confirmed its next-gen 'Project Helix' console will play PC games, with alpha hardware scheduled to go to developers from 2027, and Valve's Steam Machine starts at $1,049 for a PC that already behaves like a console.
With a console at $800 and a console-style PC at $1,049, the $1,000 self-built machine isn't the outlier it was in 2020. As another alternative, Microsoft also sells a refurbished Xbox Series S for $400, but that offers far lower performance.

title_en: How do apps on the HomeView work, and what does CarPlay have to do with it?
title_fa: How do apps on the HomeView work, and what does CarPlay have to do with it?
excerpt_en: The HomeView won't have its own App Store, but there's another method for using compatible third-party apps on the display.
excerpt_fa: The HomeView won't have its own App Store, but there's another method for using compatible third-party apps on the display.
content_en:
How do apps on the HomeView work, and what does CarPlay have to do with it?
Apple's HomeView has no App Store, but you can still use third-party apps on it.
Apple has finally announced HomeView (not HomePad), its new multimedia hub for controlling smart homes. While it runs an iOS-based operating system, it isn't exactly the same setup you have on your iPhone — although it looks quite familiar. Though on the app front, there's a major limitation: the HomeView has no App Store. But that doesn't mean third-party apps will be absent.
Instead, Apple has chosen to bring apps from a place you might not have expected: CarPlay. Yes, HomeView can run the same apps you already enjoy in your car when you pair your iPhone with a CarPlay system. It also comes with a set of pre-installed Apple apps.
HomeView will run third-party CarPlay apps
Without an App Store on its Home Screen, many people have wondered if it's possible to install third-party apps on HomeView. After all, a device that kind of looks like an iPad should be able to run iOS/iPadOS apps. Apple's own wording is somewhat vague about which apps it supports, with the HomeView page saying it "supports compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone." But after digging through the Apple Developer documentation, we now know that Apple is referring to CarPlay apps.
CarPlay doesn't run natively on your car. Instead, it mirrors the apps you have on your iPhone with a different interface. HomeView will work in pretty much the same way with third-party apps — when your iPhone is nearby, you'll be able to access compatible apps using the smart hub. Everything will be processed on your iPhone, not on HomeView.
For now, Apple says that only CarPlay audio and video apps will be available. Luckily, there are already several of them, including Spotify and Deezer. Apps in other categories, such as messaging apps and chatbots, will be left out. You don't need to download anything directly from the HomeView, and there's no way to install apps separately.
The device also comes with some Apple apps preinstalled, such as Safari, Music, Podcasts, Messages, Reminders and Calendar. Thanks to facial recognition, it can show different information depending on the person using it.
How developers can embrace HomeView (and why they might not)
For developers who already offer CarPlay-compatible apps, the work involved is minimal; those should work on HomeView with little or no effort. However, audio and video streaming apps that don't currently support CarPlay will need to add that support to work with HomeView.
Video is a good example of how important this is — iOS 27 added support for video apps on CarPlay, but none of the major players have enabled support so far. There's no Netflix, Disney+ or YouTube on CarPlay, and there won't be on HomeView either. Sure, HomeView has Safari built in, which likely means you can watch videos from the web. But the experience isn't the same as using an app.
In the short-term, HomeView gives developers new reasons to build their apps for CarPlay. This will ultimately benefit both drivers and HomeView owners, who will both gain access to new apps. But without a real App Store, it's hard to know if developers will actually want to embrace this new platform. Besides, Apple's policies for distributing CarPlay apps are much more restrictive than those for iOS apps, which might end up scaring off some developers.

title_en: Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees
title_fa: Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees
excerpt_en: The buyout offers mark Microsoft's latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce.
excerpt_fa: The buyout offers mark Microsoft's latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce.
content_en:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees, the company confirmed to TechCrunch on Monday. The move marks Microsoft’s latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce for the AI age.
Microsoft’s chief people officer, Amy Coleman, sent employees a note about the buyouts, which was also published on the company’s website.
Employees at the vice president level and below on select teams in the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom will be eligible, according to the note. Bloomberg reports that divisions including Xbox, Windows, Copilot, and Finance are participating in the buyout offer. Some employees, including those working in data centers, sales and marketing, are excluded.
The news was first reported by Business Insider.
“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” the note to employees reads. “This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support.”
The company said eligible employees would be receiving an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details on Monday. The terms of the buyout will be similar to Microsoft’s standard severance.
“The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” the note reads. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”
The buyout offer gives Microsoft a way to reduce its workforce without resorting to the more disruptive approach of mass layoffs. It’s also not the first time that the company has offered buyouts. Earlier this year, Microsoft offered buyouts to retirement-age employees, with more than 30% of the roughly 8,750 eligible workers accepting.
Microsoft’s headcount as of the end of June was 223,000.
Update 10/26/2026 11:21 AM PT: The article was updated to include additional details from Microsoft.

title_en: How to set up your phone games to play on an Android Auto screen
title_fa: How to set up your phone games to play on an Android Auto screen
excerpt_en: Soccer practice just got more bearable.
excerpt_fa: Soccer practice just got more bearable.
content_en:
How to set up your phone games to play on an Android Auto screen
Park first. Flick birds second. Soccer practice just got more bearable.
If you've wished you could play games on your car's large display rather than on your phone while waiting for your kids to finish practice at whatever sport they're into, you'll be happy to know that you can. If you've got an Android phone and Android Auto in your car, then you're set to go, as the system finally has game support.
Gaming support on Android Auto officially exited beta in September 2026, as Google invited all developers to start implementing car support for their games. Titles have already started rolling in and you can now kick back and play while your EV is charging, while your kids are at a party, or while you're having a bit of a rest on a long trip. Google says the goal is to give drivers something fun to do during downtime. Now that the doors are open to developers, your car's screen is about to get a lot more entertaining.
What games are available and can you mirror your phone?

There are also several games you might find fun like Angry Birds 2, Candy Crush Soda Saga and Beach Buggy Racing. We haven't yet reached the point where you can play Hearthstone, CoD or Super Mario Run in your car, but you can have some fun. The games must be built to recognize that your car has stopped moving, so don't expect to sneak in a round while you're at a stop light or when traffic is at a crawl. If you're parked and playing, the second you switch into gear, the game vanishes from the screen, Android Auto switches to home screen and the game icon grays out.
Unfortunately, you won't be able to just mirror your phone's screen onto Android Auto to play any game you want. Android Auto doesn't support full screen mirroring in the way some other platforms do for a couple of reasons. On one hand, this native approach ensures the games are appropriately sized for your car's display and ensures they can't circumvent safety measures. The upside is that supported games also work with controllers so you can get a more console-feel.

Connect your phone to Android Auto, either by using a USB cable or wirelessly, depending on your car. The installed games should pop up on the screen. If they don't, you should go to Settings > Connected Devices > Android Auto > Customize launcher and ensure the games you want to play are included in the launcher. It's quite easy to find and hide apps on Android Auto.
Go ahead and launch the game whenever you're parked and have some fun. If none of the titles currently compatible with Android Auto are appealing, you could also go with what's already available in Android Auto, namely GameSnacks. Not that these are particularly fantastic, but they'll get you by when you're bored.
Angry Birds 2 is just as fun to play as it is on the phone, although the bigger screen is certainly a treat, while Candy Crush Soda Saga is quite entertaining and responsive. If you're a parent and want something for the kids, there's My Talking Tom Friends. BB Racing 2 felt impossible to play since it's a game where you need to use both hands to steer the car by touching the screen. A connected controller would solve the problem if this is a game you love.
The bottom line is that you'll now have a lot more ways to stay entertained while parked, and that's a lot better than twiddling your thumbs or scrolling social media. It's another feature that might improve your Android Auto experience.

title_en: Roku apps keep crashing before you hit Play? Here's why
title_fa: Roku apps keep crashing before you hit Play? Here's why
excerpt_en: There are a few things you can try to fix it.
excerpt_fa: There are a few things you can try to fix it.
content_en:
Roku apps keep crashing before you hit Play? Here's why
There are a few things you can try to fix it.
Say what you will about Roku in light of its impending takeover by Fox, but its products are a model of simplicity. There's nothing cryptic about its hardware or software controls, and for the most part, Roku has resisted the temptation to jam its OS full of unnecessary visual flair or recommendations. You can be in your favorite streaming app in a matter of seconds.
The platform isn't bulletproof, however. Apps or Roku OS itself can still crash, which might almost be more irritating on a smart TV or media streamer than it is on a computer. Conflicts make sense on complex machines but a Roku device exists almost exclusively to stream video, perhaps with a little music thrown in for good measure. It might not feel far from your microwave refusing to make popcorn.
There are several potential reasons for Roku app crashes, most of which can be solved with one of three actions. There are scenarios, however, where more radical tactics might be needed, including even hardware upgrades. We'll try to steer you away from those.
Why your Roku apps might be crashing, and how to fix it
One possibility is that an app or the OS is buggy in some form. Although all parties try to squash as many bugs as possible, testing is never perfect, especially with so many potential hardware and software combinations out there. Normally, Roku devices update automatically whenever you do a cold boot, or leave your device on for at least 24 to 36 hours. If you want to speed things up, use your remote to navigate to Settings > System > Software update > Check Now. Keep in mind that it can take days or weeks for a patch to be developed.
If updates don't accomplish anything, try restarting your Roku via Settings > System > Power > System restart (the Power menu might be skipped on your device). This gives background processes and the system cache a fresh start, which might be all you need to deal with less severe glitches. In fact, you should be doing this periodically anyway to keep your device running as smoothly as possible.
It might also be time for general housekeeping, by which we mean deleting unused apps. Although Roku apps aren't exactly huge, even the 2024 Roku Ultra only has 4GB of storage, and older or cheaper devices may have less. You could be bumping into the swap space the OS needs, and there's no sense risking that for an app you may never open again.
When extreme measures are called for
If you've tried all of the previous steps and nothing has worked so far, your last-ditch option may be performing a factory reset. This wipes the slate completely clean, reverting your device to the state it was in out of the box — hence the name. This should be avoided whenever possible, since you'll not only have to redownload apps, but reconfigure settings and log back into your accounts. If you're sure you want to try this, head to System > Advanced system settings > Factory reset. Roku also offers hardware-based reset commands if the OS has become totally unusable.
If your device is many years old, an unfortunate possibility is that it may no longer be able to keep up with the latest software. While the company maintains surprisingly extensive update support, newer features and graphics can push the limits of RAM and processor power. You may be bumping up against these barriers, and have no choice but to buy new streaming gear.
There's only so much you can do to hold onto older software releases, unfortunately. Even when Roku has your back, streaming services may decide to cut off older app versions for the sake of security or other plans. You might as well keep updating apps as long as possible.

title_en: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
title_fa: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
excerpt_en: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, revealing soaring revenue, mounting losses, major enterprise adoption, and an unusual governance structure designed to preserve founder control and its AI safety mission.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, revealing soaring revenue, mounting losses, major enterprise adoption, and an unusual governance structure designed to preserve founder control and its AI safety mission.
content_en:
After weeks of leaked S-1s, Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.
Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.
That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”
The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.
As previously reported, Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission, will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.
The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

title_en: Apple unveils new iPad mini with OLED display and faster A20 Pro chip
title_fa: Apple unveils new iPad mini with OLED display and faster A20 Pro chip
excerpt_en: The new iPad mini features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor.
excerpt_fa: The new iPad mini features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor.
content_en:
Apple on Monday announced a new iPad mini with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display. The tablet features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor and is powered by an A20 Pro chip. The new iPad mini starts at $699 for the Wi-Fi model and $849 for the Wi-Fi and cellular model. The tech giant revealed the new device just days before its “Pro and Tell” event that’s scheduled to take place on Wednesday.
The new iPad mini is 5.4 mm in thickness, and available in two colors.
The device delivers peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits, more than twice that of the previous-generation device, along with full screen brightness of 600 nits for SDR and HDR content and a 2 million:1 contrast ratio. Apple says the iPad mini is ideal for dim-light environments.
The iPad mini also comes with a new nano-texture display option that reduces glare in bright environments, a feature already available on the iPad Pro. The updated tablet now also features a 12-megapixel center stage front camera, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support.
The Super Retina XDR display uses OLED technology for pixel-level lighting control, delivering deeper blacks, richer contrast, and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vibrant colors.
It also features an “Acoustic Display” that Apple says enhances the audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers integrated into the display deliver deeper bass and higher volume for richer sound, per the company.
The new iPad mini launches with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions, and understand what’s on their screen.
Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, the iPad mini has up to 4.5-times faster AI performance than the previous generation, according to Apple. The A20 Pro also features a 6-core CPU, delivering up to 60% faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks such as photo editing and multitasking across apps.
The device can be preordered on October 28, with availability beginning November 6.

title_en: Matiks raises $10M to expand its math and puzzle gaming platform
title_fa: Matiks raises $10M to expand its math and puzzle gaming platform
excerpt_en: Matiks has introduced a new platform for users to create games using AI.
excerpt_fa: Matiks has introduced a new platform for users to create games using AI.
content_en:
Over the past decade, head-to-head brain games like QuizUp rocketed in popularity, reaching at one point millions of users. After that, battle royale games like Fortnite and PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds had their moment in the spotlight. Lately, growth of mobile games has slowed down amid a barrage of AI content across platforms. Now, the India-based gaming company Matiks wants to steer people away from AI-riddled timelines with its math, logic, and brain-game puzzle platform.
The namesake app has been around for two years, but has seen real traction this year. The startup said that its daily users have grown from 22,000 earlier in the year to over 300,000 by September. The app also saw 2.2 million monthly active users in that month, with the company’s growth attracting fresh investor interest.
The startup said Monday that it has raised $10 million in pre-Series A funding led by General Catalyst, with participation from Indian entrepreneur Ronnie Screwvala and existing investors InfoEdge Ventures, Tanglin Venture Partners, and Untitled Ventures. With this round, the company has raised over $13.5 million to date.
Matiks was founded by Sudhanshu Bhatia, Mohan Kumar, and Sushant Timmapur, who were college friends. Bhatia, who has a background in competitive mental math, said that he started working on the idea while he was working at American Express on an anti-money laundering strategy.
“For the last 10 years, the platforms have made entertainment consumption easy, but much of it is brain slop. We started exploring how we can make math-related games fun and entertaining like the other content,” Bhatia told TechCrunch over a call.
“Since I’ve had this background in mental math, I knew that a competitive ecosystem exists there. We got to know that the same exists for puzzles and memory. We wanted to make our app as entertaining as physical sports, so we opted for a dual format,” said Bhatia.
In the app, users can choose from Math, Puzzle, Memory, and Logic categories and play different games against bots to practice, and then against real players. Users can also play challenges and quests to earn points, maintain streaks, and unlock new games.
I have been playing the games for more than a week, and they are a good distraction for me, as I like games I can finish in a few minutes. The app hasn’t pushed me much toward purchasing more in-game items or shown distasteful ad pop-ups that would prompt me to uninstall the app completely.
Until now, Matiks has been focusing on user growth and just started testing a subscription this month, which unlocks game analysis, tips and tricks, practice, and additional features. The startup also allows for in-game purchases to skip certain challenges, maintain a streak, and boost XP points.
Bhatia said that while the majority of the game’s players are based in India, the startup has seen traction from other markets like the U.S., South Korea, and Japan. The startup plans to bring in localization to grow the latter two markets.
While Matiks is battling against AI slop, it isn’t entirely rejecting AI. The company has debuted an experimental game-creation platform called Jelo, which lets users make their own games and lets others play them. There is a ton of competition in this area, including Google’s new platform called Playground.
The startup, with 41 full-time employees, wants to use the funding to scale this platform by expanding into newer markets.
Rahul Humayun, a partner at General Catalyst, told TechCrunch in an email that the product’s pace of iteration and user engagement have given the firm encouraging signs.
“We found the Matiks vision, product, and most importantly the community to be truly N of 1. The team’s product taste and pace of iteration made it a no-brainer,” said Humayun. The exceptional product love and power user behaviour are clear signs that the team is onto something special. We believe these are strong leading indicators for monetisation, with early results looking promising. The depth of engagement across surface areas like duels, social, Snac, and now creation only helps.”

title_en: Tesla turns to Turo to boost adoption of Full Self-Driving (Supervised)
title_fa: Tesla turns to Turo to boost adoption of Full Self-Driving (Supervised)
excerpt_en: Eligible Turo hosts will also get a one-month free trial of Tesla's FSD software.
excerpt_fa: Eligible Turo hosts will also get a one-month free trial of Tesla's FSD software.
content_en:
Car rental giant Turo will start advertising which Teslas on its marketplace are outfitted with the automaker’s advanced driver assistance system, Full Self-Driving (Supervised) — or FSD, a collaboration that could boost further adoption of the driving software.
Eligible Turo “hosts” who rent their cars on the platform will also receive a free one-month trial of FSD. Turo said it is working with Tesla to directly access the automaker’s API to verify which cars have FSD enabled.
The announcement comes just a few days after Tesla offered updated figures that show the carmaker is finally getting more customers to pay for the software, which can handle most driving tasks but still requires human supervision.
Last week, Tesla revealed that around 1.7 million customers have paid for FSD globally, out of more than 10 million cars built and sold to date. The company said more than 75% of customers who took delivery of a car in North America during the third-quarter paid for an FSD subscription. That was a roughly 20% increase from the second quarter, though the company’s U.S. sales have been in decline.
Tesla has spent much of the last year re-working some of its showrooms to focus more on FSD as a selling point. In a post last week, the company’s chief executive Elon Musk said the effort is working.
“People are buying FSD with a car attached, not the other way around,” wrote Musk.

title_en: The best apps for tracking your reading and discovering new books
title_fa: The best apps for tracking your reading and discovering new books
excerpt_en: There are numerous apps on the market that promise to do just that, so we’ve compiled a list of some of the best ones to help you pick the right one for you.
excerpt_fa: There are numerous apps on the market that promise to do just that, so we’ve compiled a list of some of the best ones to help you pick the right one for you.
content_en:
From discovering new books and organizing your reading list to tracking your reading goal and sharing recommendations, book apps make it easier to maintain reading as a hobby. There are numerous apps on the market that promise to do just that, so we’ve compiled a list of some of the best ones to help you pick the right one for you. Whether you’re an occasional reader or a dedicated bookworm, these apps can help you make the most of your reading journey.
Some of the apps on this list are somewhat new, while others have been around for a few years. Amazon-owned Goodreads, which is arguably the most popular book-related app, isn’t included in this list because we’re focusing on newer, lesser-known platforms.
Fable
Fable is a reading app that combines book tracking with a social platform. It lets you organize reading lists, set reading goals, track streaks, write reviews, and join virtual book clubs. You also get personalized book recommendations and the chance to discuss what you’re reading with other readers.
The app differs from others on this list because it puts reading and community at the forefront of the platform, which makes it a great option for people who like staying motivated to read by being part of a community and discussing their reads.
Fable is free to download on iOS and Android, but also offers a Fable Plus subscription tier that unlocks additional features like custom goals and advanced analytics for a monthly fee of $5.99.
Bookshelf
Bookshelf is a reading app designed to help people organize their libraries, discover new books, and remember more of what they read. The app positions itself as an alternative to Goodreads, and combines traditional reading logs with AI-powered recommendations and tools.
You can create custom shelves, set reading goals, receive reminders, save favorite quotes, and access AI-generated book summaries, key insights, and thematic analyses to recall the books you’ve read and get a deeper understanding of them.
Bookshelf is free to download on iOS, but offers a $6.99 monthly fee to unlock premium features like unlimited collections and enhanced analytics.
Pagebound
Pagebound is a book app that lets readers track their books, create lists, set goals, and discuss individual titles in dedicated forums. Instead of having to join an actual book club group, users can post reactions and thoughts to connect with others reading the same title.
You don’t have to worry about spoilers for the end of the book, as conversations are organized based on reading progress, allowing readers to share theories and thoughts as they read. The app is a great option for people who want to discuss their reads with others without having to commit to a scheduled book club.
Pagebound is free to download on iOS and Android and offers a $9.99 monthly subscription for added features like profile customization.
StoryGraph
StoryGraph is a reading app that lets users track their reading, discover new books, and access detailed reading statistics and personalized recommendations. Users can set reading goals, join reading challenges, and find new titles based on their preferred moods, themes, genres, and pacing.
The app is ideal for readers who want to better understand their reading habits and discover books that match their current interests. Its recommendation system doesn’t solely rely on what’s popular or trending, and instead caters to exactly what readers are looking for.
StoryGraph is free to use on iOS and Android, but also offers a paid subscription called StoryGraph Plus that costs $4.99 per month and unlocks custom charts, additional statistics, and more.
Margins
Margins is a great option for mood readers, as it offers mood-based discovery alongside a more focused reading experience. It helps users find their next read based on how they feel in the moment by searching for specific vibes, such as “books like 1920s Paris.” Users can also track their reading goals.
The app also lets users customize their virtual library by choosing book covers that match their aesthetic and organizing their shelves in different ways, including by color. For users who enjoy a more immersive experience, Margins offers a built-in “Reading Time” meditation timer that blocks social media apps.

title_en: Fitbit Air vs. Whoop: Which screenless fitness tracker is better for you?
title_fa: Fitbit Air vs. Whoop: Which screenless fitness tracker is better for you?
excerpt_en: How locked in do you want to be?
excerpt_fa: How locked in do you want to be?
content_en:
Fitbit Air vs. Whoop: Which screenless fitness tracker is better for you?
How locked in do you want to be?
Screenless trackers are all the rage right now, even though they've existed for decades. For instance, Whoop launched its first tracker in 2015, launching as among the first, if not the first of the category. In March, Whoop raised $575 million, garnering itself a $10 billion valuation, signaling increased interest in the space. But Whoop is now facing competition from companies like Garmin, Luna, Hume, Amazfit and, most notably, Google with its Fitbit Air (see our Fitbit Air review). In fact, Google teased it was preparing something like the Air on March 31 — the same day as Whoop's funding announcement. Whether or not the timing was coincidental, the Fitbit Air is quite obviously Google's take on Whoop and the category of screenless health trackers.
The Whoop MG is one of the company's newest, so it makes sense to compare that to the Fitbit Air. To determine which of these two is the better option for you, I've compared both devices on features and pricing. In short, they both do a great job of tracking activities, sleep, and vitals, and offering a comprehensive and informative app experience. But they also both require a subscription to get the most out of your data.
Key differences between them
The Fitbit Air is slimmer than Whoop bands, which has an impact on battery life. Newer Whoop models like the Whoop 5.0 and Whoop MG are rated to last 14+ days while Google says the Fitbit Air lasts up to seven. You can squeeze more hours out of the newer Whoop bands with a convenient wireless battery pack that you can slide onto the band to charge on the go. It adds bulk to your wrist but you never have to remove the band to recharge it as long as you keep the battery packed topped up.
The companion apps for both companies provide tons of data about activities, sleep and vitals. They also each have an AI assistant you can call on to log meals, ask for advice and even use to build a wellness and workout plan. But the Whoop app can be overwhelming at first. It's better suited to those who are serious about health, wellness and especially fitness, monitoring things like strain and recovery. Whoop also captures heart rate data at a higher sampling frequency. On the other hand, the Fitbit Air's Google Health app is more user-friendly for the average person.
While you can get away without a subscription with the Fitbit Air, getting just basic tracking, Whoop works on a membership setup and you can't use it without one. Sign up for a membership and the hardware is included. According to Whoop, "Whoop One will be sold on WHOOP 5.0 hardware in the US, MX, CA, EU and UK. WHOOP One in these regions will be sold at $199/ year." Outside of those regions, however, it's worth pointing out that the company says "Whoop One memberships are provided with a certified pre-owned 4.0 sensor and Onyx Superknit Band." If you have any issue with using pre-owned products, this might be of concern.
By contrast, the Fitbit Air comes with a three-month trial to Google Health Premium after which you can cancel or continue by paying a small fee. A Whoop membership starts at about $149 for the first year ($199 after the first year) or, for those already paying monthly, $25 per month. Meanwhile, Google Health Premium will set you back $100 per year (with an annual plan or $10 per month) on top of the hardware cost of $100.
The highest tier Whoop subscription is $359 annually! So, Whoop is better suited for serious athletes and the Fitbit Air for everyday users or casual fitness buffs.
Which should you buy?
The advantage with Fitbit Air is that even without a subscription, you still get basic health insights and activity tracking, including sleep tracking. What you miss out on is AI-driven features like the personal assistance, guidance, and training plans, along with access to workouts and deeper sleep insights. But if you're happy just to check in to see if you got a good's night sleep, how your vitals are and to log your daily walks and workouts, it's perfectly fine on its own. Plus, if you have a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription, Google Health Premium comes as one of the perks.
Whoop's devices are higher-end, premium trackers, but there is no option to get one without a pricey membership. It has all the same sensors and the app works similarly, albeit with much more granular data about things like strain and recovery. Whoop even plans to offer in-app video consultations with licensed clinicians in participating locations. In my experience, I have noticed that Whoop is better at automatically detecting activities, which is useful for those who do strength training or intense cardio and don't want to have to manually start and stop a workout.
If you decide to pay for Google Health Premium with the Fitbit Air, that tracker offers a more engaging and conversational AI Coach experience. There is AI support with Whoop, but Google's version feels more natural, whether you want to tell it to log your coffee and oatmeal in the morning or advise about your sore shoulder and ask it to modify your training plan accordingly to accommodate. Overall, the Fitbit Air is the better and more affordable device for most people. But for those with deeper pockets who are undergoing intense training, a Whoop tracker might be worth it.

title_en: Can you run regular Ethernet cables outside?
title_fa: Can you run regular Ethernet cables outside?
excerpt_en: Just because you can do something doesn't mean you should.
excerpt_fa: Just because you can do something doesn't mean you should.
content_en:
Can you run regular Ethernet cables outside?
Just because you can do something doesn't mean you should.
Cable category terms like Cat5e and Cat6 have that industrial twang, so, understandably, some may assume they're tough enough for outdoor use. And they can do more than just improve home internet, which is especially helpful for security cameras on your porch or in your yard. Sure, you can use standard Ethernet cables outdoors, but you can also run outside in a lightning storm with a ten-foot metal pole above your head — just because you can do something doesn't mean you should. Standard indoor cables have a flexible PVC jacket, which is susceptible to sunlight. Over time it will fade and crack, exposing the internal components and ultimately degrading the connection.
Outside temperatures and rain accelerate the problem. The copper in an Ethernet cable won't have proper protection from lightning strikes and other elements. Use a cable specifically rated for outdoor exposure, such as a direct-burial-rated cable made for an in-ground run across the yard. Direct-burial cables are specifically designed for this, and it will be written clearly on the cable jacket. Whatever the cable rating, it's best practice to install surge protection on either end of the cable. While it requires additional hardware, you can avoid the risks of running copper outdoors by using outdoor-rated fiber optic cables instead of Ethernet, though any equipment exposed to the elements would still be at risk.
Use the right outdoor cable
There's a difference between a direct-burial and an outdoor Ethernet cable. Outdoor cables typically use a more weather-resistant polyethylene jacket (such as LLDPE or PE) instead of the standard PVC jacket. These materials are much better at resisting UV exposure, moisture, and wild temperature swings.
If the cable needs to run underground, opt for the direct-burial cable. These cables are capable of dealing with long-term exposure to moisture and the physical pressure of the surrounding soil. Depending on the type of direct-burial cable, it might use water-blocking tape, powder, or gel to keep the wire dry even if the outer jacket is damaged.
Local ordinances may not be happy with your buried wire, so be sure to check local rules on conduit, depth, and the cable types permitted. If all you need is a short and simple exterior run to an outdoor access point, a Cat6 outdoor-rated Ethernet cable is appropriate. Always secure exterior cable runs with cable clips to avoid abrasion, and never sharply bend the cable, even if that means the run requires a bit of creativity.
How to tell if an Ethernet cable is outdoor-rated
To make sure your cable can be used outside, check the printing on it. It's not always easy to read the small print, especially if it's faded a bit, so you might have to make an extra effort for it; the color or category label means nothing where this is concerned. Terms like "CMX," "OSP," "UV-resistant," "sunlight-resistant," or simply "outdoor" are what to look for. Outdoor cables will also often list their jacket material, such as PE, HDPE, or LLDPE. The National Electrical Code (NEC) requires communications cables installed in buildings to be listed and marked, and UL's guidance notes that cable evaluated for outdoor use is marked "outdoor" or "outdoor use," so the rating shouldn't be hard to confirm. Plus, the documentation that comes with them will state that they're approved for direct burial or wet locations.
Just note that an outdoor-rated cable doesn't mean its inherent toughness makes it an excellent indoor application. Some exterior cables may not meet the requirements for indoor fire safety hazards, and that includes situations where only a small section of the outdoor cable is run inside. An unlisted outdoor cable generally can't run more than 50 feet inside before it needs to terminate and transition to an indoor-rated cable, and shorter is better. Your best bet is to always read the cable's markings and any associated literature. If you're still unsure, check the local codes, especially for a permanent installation.

title_en: Which Android phone is the closest equivalent to the iPhone Duo?
title_fa: Which Android phone is the closest equivalent to the iPhone Duo?
excerpt_en: Can we find the iPhone Duo's perfect Android match?
excerpt_fa: Can we find the iPhone Duo's perfect Android match?
content_en:
Which Android phone is the closest equivalent to the iPhone Duo?
There are plenty of non-Apple foldables out there, but finding a perfect match is tricky.
While Apple's first-ever foldable phone is the subject of plenty of attention, the Cupertino tech giant was actually well behind Android phone makers to the category. The Duo makes a strong entrance, but with major players like Samsung, Google and Motorola at it for years, there is no shortage of foldable smartphones in this day and age.
Each of these three competitors offers a book-style foldable phone, like the Duo, which essentially turns any smartphone into a mini tablet. As they're larger than the alternative flip-phone designs, they're a great choice for multitasking, reading, streaming shows and more.
Even when we limit the focus of this article on the passport-style options, there's no clear-cut Android counterpart for the Duo. Each of the candidates differs on size, cameras, durability and more. Still, we can look at specs from the iPhone Duo's biggest competitors and do our best to determine which is the closest match.
Display sizes, cameras and durability
Let's start with display sizes. The Duo's 5.4-inch outer screen and 7.6-inch inner display sit in the middle of the pack. The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the nearest match, with its 7.6-inch interior display and 5.5-inch cover screen.
Meanwhile, Google goes bigger than both, with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold boasting an 8-inch inner display and a 6.5-inch outer screen. Motorola's Razr Fold is the biggest of the bunch, with a 6.6-inch cover screen and a nearly 8.1-inch inner display.
These three smartphones are all lighter than the Duo, which weighs in at 9 ounces. For reference, the Z Fold 8 is 7.09 ounces, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 8.4 ounces and the Razr Fold is 8.6 ounces.
As for cameras, the Duo's 12-megapixel Center Stage front camera and pair of 48MP rear cameras are narrowly outmatched by the Z Fold 8. Samsung's latest foldable features two 50MP cameras, but the one up front is 10MP. In some regard, the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a close match, with a 48MP main camera like Apple's. The big difference is that Google's flagship foldable also includes a 10.8MP telephoto lens, while the Duo lacks one.
On sheer megapixel count alone, Motorola's Razr Fold outdoes the others with 50MP main, ultrawide and telephoto cameras and a 20MP cover selfie camera.
Considering these devices tend to cost a lot more than the average phone, durability might (rightfully) be one of your biggest concerns. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is the only one of the Android foldables we're comparing to match Apple's IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Razr Fold land at IP48 and IP48/IP49 respectively.
Battery life and starting price
Battery life is trickier to compare, since Apple hasn't disclosed the Duo's precise battery capacity, only that it can endure up to 24 hours of mixed use on a charge. We have more concrete numbers with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8, as we know they have 4,806mAh and 4,800mAh batteries respectively. The Razr Fold features a 6,000mAh battery, which Motorola says is "the largest available in a foldable."
Starting prices are closer than you'd expect. The Duo starts at $1,999.99 for 256GB, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (256GB), Pixel 11 Pro Fold (256GB) and Razr Fold (512GB) all start at $1,899.99. As for storage, Google and Samsung offer the closest capacities to Apple, with both their foldables available in a 1TB option. However, neither offers a 2TB configuration like the Duo.
Of options readily available in the US, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is about as close as it gets to the iPhone Duo at first glance, with a similarly sized 7.6-inch display, two 50MP rear sensors and a slightly less-sharp selfie camera.
Beyond the big names
Outside of these major players, it's worth mentioning that Xiaomi revealed its 18 Fold just days before the Duo, touting it as the brand's first "mid-size" foldable. Its display measures 7.68 inches when unfolded, combined with a 5.38-inch outer display. These measurements come very close to the Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. The sad part? Like most Xiaomi smartphones, the 18 Fold isn't distributed stateside.

title_en: Why Google chrome is always using so much RAM
title_fa: Why Google chrome is always using so much RAM
excerpt_en: Chrome is known for being a memory hog, but it may be more urban myth than reality. Here's how Google Chrome manages RAM.
excerpt_fa: Chrome is known for being a memory hog, but it may be more urban myth than reality. Here's how Google Chrome manages RAM.
content_en:
Why Google chrome is always using so much RAM
Chrome has developed a reputation for being a memory hog, but is it deserved?
If you have spent any time on the internet, you have probably come across the "fact" that Chrome is a RAM hog. However, this isn't a fact so much as it is an internet meme. It has more to do with jokes about browsing and less to do with actual data, same as the claim that Microsoft Edge is slow and out of date. Both have been repeated so often that they started to feel true.
This isn't to say that Chrome doesn't use as much RAM as it needs; it absolutely does. It just means that RAM usage isn't that much of an issue in 2026, nor was it that much of an issue back in 2016.
What Chrome is actually doing with your RAM
Websites, and the way we use them, have changed considerably since the early days of the internet. Browsing the web used to be about moving from one text-heavy page to another, with occasional photos or videos sprinkled in. Websites today more closely resemble apps than simple web pages. Each holds more information and allows for a much more versatile browsing experience, while the browser itself is expected to hold multiple tabs at once while also running several extensions in the background.
All of those features together add up, and they are all expected to load instantly and run smoothly. That means the creators of the browser need to make a decision: share memory and processes across tabs to save RAM, or give each tab and site its own process, which costs more memory but keeps things fast and stable. Google Chrome, much like many other browsers out there, chooses the latter. And that's a good thing.
Why that's good for you
By giving each website its own dedicated process inside the computer's memory, Chrome doesn't just make sure your browsing stays fast and responsive. It also prevents browser-wide crashes. Anyone old enough to remember the early days of web browsing probably remembers the terrible feeling when your browser suddenly disappeared along with all of your work, while you were left staring at a small system message telling you the browser had encountered a problem and had to shut down.
Browsers today avoid this problem by keeping each site in its own process. One crashed site does not bring down the entire browser, along with the 20+ other tabs you had open. This approach also helps with security. Chrome runs each site in a sandboxed process, and the operating system keeps those processes apart, so a malicious page can't easily peek at what's happening in your banking or email tab. Some of that extra memory is the price of that wall between your tabs, and it's a price most people would be glad to pay.
Why RAM isn't the main factor in browsing
There is a common misconception that RAM usage should be kept as low as possible so the computer runs smoother. In reality, unused RAM is wasted RAM. The whole point of memory is to hold everything you want running fast and smoothly, and a browser that fills it with pages, media and prepared tabs is doing its job. PCMag says 8GB of RAM should be fine for most general-use PCs, several times what a single browser typically needs, so the headroom is there to be used.
High usage isn't the only warning sign — you could also have a memory leak. A memory leak is when a program grabs memory and never gives it back, so the number keeps climbing for no good reason. Chrome's built-in Task Manager (Shift + Esc) shows which tab or extension is the culprit.
If you're still worried, there are some alternatives
Chrome has its own answer built in. Memory Saver puts tabs you haven't touched in a while to sleep and frees up the memory they were using, then reloads them when you click back. Google has since rolled it out to everyone. You can find it in Chrome's settings under Performance, and you can add sites that should never be put to sleep, such as the one playing your music.
Other browsers take a different route. Microsoft Edge runs on the same Chromium foundation as Chrome, so it uses a similar process model, but its sleeping tabs and Energy Saver put idle tabs to sleep to cut memory use. Firefox groups tabs into fewer shared processes and unloads tabs when your system runs low on memory. Both are reasonable choices, and neither is a cure. A browser that gives you the same experience for a fraction of the memory would have to give up something on the way.
Chrome shouldn't feel sluggish
If Chrome feels slow, don't just look at the memory number. Open the browser's Task Manager and look for a tab or extension that keeps growing. If nothing does, Chrome is using your RAM the way it's meant to, and you can leave it alone. If things still feel sluggish, the cause may be somewhere else entirely, such as a nearly full drive or a slow connection, and restarting the browser is a good first step.
